text: Project documentsArchitecture Code

Overview
The project estimates excess Medicare cost after cryptococcosis in kidney transplant recipients, using USRDS data (linked UNOS and Medicare) accessed through the separate usRds package. It works in four stages:

Build a time-varying cohort of transplant recipients.
Match each case at diagnosis to up to number_controls_per_case (2) never-diagnosed controls, using risk-set matching on time since transplant.
Turn each person’s claims into an inflation-adjusted cost panel by month, from month −3 to month 11 around the index date.
Fit cost models in which patient_type × month gives the case–control cost difference.

A Quarto website in quarto/ explains each script and displays its code in eval: false chunks. The site never runs the analysis: the only script sections it runs are the Setup page’s constants and ICD code lists, which define values and read nothing. It is rendered by .github/workflows/publish.yml and published to the gh-pages branch, which GitHub Pages serves; the local render in docs/ is not committed.

Hidden dependencies
Some functions read globals instead of taking them as arguments:

calculate_number_potential_matches() reads medicare_history, created in create_cohort.R.
plot_mean_monthly_costs() defaults countdf = final_count_df, created in postmatch_processing.R. R evaluates the default only when the function is called, so this works from figures.R but not earlier.

Cases enter at diagnosis, so a case’s first row has tstart equal to the days from their most recent transplant to diagnosis. That value is their matching time. Controls run from TX1DATE to terminal_date.

Details that are easy to miss:

IN_REV feeds only the 365-day totals. The monthly panel and all models use IN_CLM and PS_REV; grand_total_cost_month is IN_CLM_month_total + PS_REV_month_total.
Monthly sums are floored at 0 with pmax(), which absorbs negative adjustment claims.
final_count_df (persons per group per month) is the risk table under each monthly plot.

Known Architectural Gaps
Status as of commit 8a52330. These come from reading the code and need checking against the real data where noted.

Matched-set ID is lost before modeling. matched_control_indices is a list column, and final_data_set drops list columns. Models can cluster only on USRDS_ID. (Needs a design decision.)
Death is not an input to end_date_analysis. DIED appears only in the follow_up_final_event label. Post-death months stay in the panel unless a coverage end date already equals the death date. (Needs verification: count person-months after DIED by patient_type.)
Open items from earlier reviews, still present: calculate_total_excess_costs() sums months −2 and −1 interactions; slice_head(n = 1) makes set.seed() ineffective; the potential-match count checks coverage at a different date than the loop; controls are limited to never-diagnosed patients; graft status isn’t matched; cases with zero controls are still added as matched.
Partly fixed: temp_formula and fit are now initialized; the unused GEE tweedie block at the end of modeling.R still runs when sourced.

Definition

Transplant recipient with an incident cryptococcosis claim meeting the cohort criteria; index date is the diagnosis date


Potential control
Transplant recipient with no cryptococcosis diagnosis at any time

Floor of days from index divided by 30; panel covers −3 to 11

Days observed in a panel month, capped at 30; used as the model offset

title: Clinical background
text: This page summarizes what is known about cryptococcosis in kidney transplant recipients and about its cost, and the gap this study addresses. How the study answers its question is set out under Study design and methods.

title: Clinical background
text:
Cryptococcosis after kidney transplant
Cryptococcosis is the third most common invasive fungal infection in solid organ transplant recipients1. In a multicenter US surveillance network, it accounted for 8% of invasive fungal infections in organ transplant recipients, and kidney recipients had the lowest one-year incidence of any invasive fungal infection of all organ types2. In inpatient data from three US states, 0.32% of kidney recipients had cryptococcosis coded during follow-up3. Earlier, in USRDS data from 1994 to 1997, cryptococcosis was among the leading causes of hospitalized fungal infection after kidney transplant4.
Most infections occur well after transplant. Median onset was 616 days after kidney transplant in the three-state cohort3, and 575 days for cryptococcosis across organ types in the surveillance network2. Among kidney recipients hospitalized for cryptococcosis in a national USRDS cohort, the median time from the most recent transplant to the index hospitalization was 30.5 months5.
Transmission through the donated organ is rare. From 2009 to 2019, US reports to the transplant network’s disease-transmission committee identified 12 donors with proven or probable transmission, to 23 recipients; for another 11 donors, recipients received prophylaxis and transmission was averted6. Donor-derived infection usually presents early after transplant6, so it is context for this study rather than its focus.

title: Clinical background
text:
Presentation, treatment and outcomes
Onset can be insidious1, and the central nervous system is often involved: in a national USRDS cohort of 1,265 kidney recipients hospitalized for cryptococcosis from 2006 to 2016, 51% had meningitis5. Guidelines recommend lumbar puncture for suspected or proven disease, and treatment of meningitis or disseminated disease with induction therapy, a lipid formulation of amphotericin B with flucytosine, followed by consolidation with fluconazole1; a 2024 global guideline updates these recommendations across patient groups7. US guidelines recommend at least 2 weeks of induction and at least 8 weeks of consolidation8, so treatment lasts at least 10 weeks. Lipid formulations of amphotericin B were associated with lower 90-day mortality than the deoxycholate formulation in transplant recipients with central nervous system disease9. Reducing immunosuppression during treatment can lead to immune reconstitution syndrome1, which has been linked to graft loss in kidney recipients10.
Outcomes are poor. In the national USRDS cohort, 22% of kidney recipients hospitalized for cryptococcosis died within six months, 44% required intensive care and 49% had acute kidney injury5. In a prospective multicenter cohort of 111 organ transplant recipients, 61% had disseminated disease and 14% died within 90 days; mortality was lower in those receiving a calcineurin inhibitor11. In a French cohort of 88 kidney recipients diagnosed from 2002 to 2020, 33% died within 12 months, and about a third of recipients lost their graft by last follow-up, with or without meningitis12.

title: Clinical background
section: What is known about its cost
text:
What is known about its cost
Published US estimates are of hospital stays, of modelled treatment, or of costs over time without a comparison group:

Per hospitalization. National estimates put cryptococcosis at 4,755 hospitalizations in 2014, with mean payments per stay of about $39,000 to $70,000 depending on the payer (in 2017 dollars)13. In inpatient data from 18 states for 1997 to 2009, median costs per hospitalization for cryptococcal meningitis were about $15,700 to $16,800, depending on HIV status14.
Excess cost compared with similar patients. Two studies compared patients with and without fungal infection, with all fungal species together: about $55,400 in excess cost per hospital stay in transplant recipients with invasive fungal infection, in national inpatient data for 2004 and 200515; and an average attributable cost of $31,200 per patient for systemic fungal infections, including cryptococcosis, from inpatient costs and modelled outpatient costs for 199816.
Treatment. A cost-effectiveness model estimated costs of care for cryptococcal meningitis of about $45,000 to $83,000 depending on the induction regimen, at 2015 US prices, when flucytosine cost about $2,000 a day in the United States8.
Over time. In commercial claims, patients with cryptococcal meningitis accrued mean charges of $103,236 over up to five years after diagnosis, with no comparison group and in charges rather than payments17.

Excess Medicare cost after other infections in kidney transplant recipients has been estimated in USRDS data. Pneumonia or sepsis in the first year after transplant added about $40,000 to $50,000 in first-year Medicare payments18. We found no study that estimates the excess Medicare payments attributable to cryptococcosis over the months after diagnosis in kidney transplant recipients, compared with similar recipients at the same time since transplant.

title: Clinical background
text:
Why this question matters
An estimate of the cost attributable to cryptococcosis over the months after diagnosis, rather than of one hospital stay, is what payers and transplant programs need to judge its burden, and what economic models need when weighing prevention, such as donor screening or prophylaxis, against treatment. Costs may also begin before the recorded diagnosis: in state inpatient data, a third of HIV-negative patients hospitalized with cryptococcosis had a hospital admission suggestive of the disease in the preceding 90 days19. The study’s monthly cost profile begins three months before diagnosis.
This study asks: among adult kidney transplant recipients, how much more does Medicare pay in the 12 months after cryptococcosis is diagnosed than for similar recipients at the same time since transplant who have not been diagnosed? Study design and methods explains how it is answered.

title: Setup

The analysis relies on a set of open-source R packages for data management, cohort construction, visualization, and statistical modeling. These libraries were selected based on their stability, community support, and suitability for large-scale longitudinal health data.

library(tidyverse)
library(lubridate)

#Core library for the USRDS
library(usRds)

#Flowchart libraries
library(strobe)
library(flowchart)

#Table libraries
library(gt)
library(gtsummary)

#Plotting libraries
library(ggplot2)
library(ggbeeswarm)
library(patchwork)

#Statistical modeling libraries
library(glmmTMB)
library(emmeans)
library(geepack)
library(broom)
library(broom.mixed)
library(multcomp)

title: Setup
text:
Constants
A number of analysis parameters are reused across cohort construction, matching, and cost modeling steps.
These constants are defined in the R/setup.R file.


Click to show/hide R Code
#Constants
censor_date<-as.Date("2022-01-01")
minimum_followup<-1 #Minimum followup in days
maximum_followup<-365 #Maximum followup in days
number_controls_per_case<-2 #Number of controls per case
inflation_month<-"January"
inflation_year<-2021
baseline_months_cost<-3 #N
full_months <- -baseline_months_cost:11 #Range of months for longitudinal analysis

title: Modeling
text:
Longitudinal cost data models
The following code runs models on the following outcomes as generated by the files in the R/postmatch_processing.R file, to calculate costs per month:

Total costs
Physician/supplier costs
Institutional total claims costs
Institutional Home Health costs
Institutional Inpatient costs
Institutional Outpatient costs
Institutional Skilled Nursing Facility costs
Institutional Dialysis costs
Institutional Auxiliary costs
Institutional Hospice costs

Analyzing cost data is notoriously challenging1. The VA Health Economics Resource Center has a practical guide, and whole textbooks cover the topic2.
To account for the repeated-observations nature of the data, both generalized estimating equations3 and mixed-effects models with patient as a random effect4 were explored.
Medical cost data are highly skewed, with many zeros. We explored linear models, log(cost) models5 and Tweedie models6.
Accounting for costs that are incomplete because follow-up ends, through loss of coverage or death, is itself a challenging topic, reviewed for health services researchers by Wijeysundera and colleagues7. Seminal methods papers include Lin and colleagues8 and Bang et al.
We trialed multiple types of models:

Naive estimation (patients do not contribute observations if uncovered or dead)
Treating post-death costs as zero, ignoring months with costs uncovered (note: not done yet)
Treating post-death costs as zero, weighting to adjust for uncovered months (note: not done yet)



Click to show/hide R Code
# Statistical modeling of cost data

temp_formula <- list()
fit <- list()

for (outcome in c("grand_total_cost_month", "IN_CLM_month_total", "PS_REV_month_total", "IN_CLM_month_groupedHomeHealth",
                  "IN_CLM_month_groupedHospice","IN_CLM_month_groupedNonclaimauxiliary","IN_CLM_month_groupedDialysis",
                  "IN_CLM_month_groupedOutpatient","IN_CLM_month_groupedInpatient","IN_CLM_month_groupedSkilledNursingFacility")){

  temp_formula[["glmmTMB"]][["untransformed"]]<-as.formula(
    paste0(
      outcome, " ~ ",
      "patient_type * factor(month) + ",
      "offset(log(month_offset)) + ",
      "(1 | USRDS_ID)"
    )
  )
  temp_formula[["gee"]][["untransformed"]]<-as.formula(
    paste0(
      outcome, " ~ ",
      "patient_type * factor(month) + ",
      "offset(log(month_offset))"
    )
  )

  temp_formula[["glmmTMB"]][["logtransformed"]] <- as.formula(
    paste0(
      "log1p(", outcome, ") ~ ",
      "patient_type * factor(month) + ",
      "offset(log(month_offset)) + ",
      "(1 | USRDS_ID)"
    )
  )
  temp_formula[["gee"]][["logtransformed"]]<-as.formula(
    paste0(
      "log1p(", outcome, ") ~ ",
      "patient_type * factor(month) + ",
      "offset(log(month_offset))"
    )
  )
  
  message(
    "Fitting models to formula: ", temp_formula[["glmmTMB"]][["untransformed"]]
  )
  
  message("Fitting glmmTMB to tweedie family...")
  fit[[outcome]][["glmmTMB"]][["tweedie"]] <- glmmTMB(
    temp_formula[["glmmTMB"]][["untransformed"]],
    family = tweedie(link = "log"),
    data = final_data_set
  )
  
  message("Fitting glmmTMB to linear family...")
  fit[[outcome]][["glmmTMB"]][["linear"]] <- glmmTMB(
    temp_formula[["glmmTMB"]][["untransformed"]],
    family = gaussian(link = "identity"),
    data = final_data_set
  )
  
  message("Fitting gee to linear family...")
  fit[[outcome]][["gee"]][["linear"]] <- geeglm(
    temp_formula[["gee"]][["untransformed"]],
    id     = USRDS_ID,
    data   = final_data_set,
    corstr = "exchangeable",
    family = gaussian(link = "identity"))  
  
  message(
    "Fitting models to formula: ", temp_formula[["glmmTMB"]][["logtransformed"]]
  )
  
  message("Fitting glmmTMB to logcost family...")
  fit[[outcome]][["glmmTMB"]][["log"]] <- glmmTMB(
    temp_formula[["glmmTMB"]][["logtransformed"]],
    family = gaussian(link = "identity"),
    data = final_data_set
  )
  
  message("Fitting gee to logcost family...")
  fit[[outcome]][["gee"]][["log"]] <- geeglm(
    temp_formula[["gee"]][["logtransformed"]],
    id     = USRDS_ID,
    data   = final_data_set,
    corstr = "exchangeable",
    family = gaussian(link = "identity"))  

  
}

title: Create cohort
section: Initial data loading and preprocessing of USRDS core and transplant files
text:
Initial data loading and preprocessing of USRDS core and transplant files
This portion of the code imports the USRDS files needed for the cryptococcus analysis. It makes use of the load_usrds_file() function from the usRds package as well as several tidyverse cleaning functions.
Key files used:

patients: part of the USRDS Core data set, with one record per patient and basic demographic and kidney-failure data, including transplant and death dates1.
tx: also part of the Core data set, with one record per kidney transplant. USRDS reconciles these records from CMS and OPTN sources, and they include the transplant date and the date of graft failure1.
txunos_trr_ki and txunos_trr_kp: part of the USRDS Transplant data set. These are the OPTN (Organ Procurement and Transplantation Network) transplant recipient registration records for kidney and kidney–pancreas transplants, collected by OPTN since 19871.

The code below loads and merges transplant records across the core and OPTN files, constructs a cumulative transplant count per patient, and reshapes the data into a time-varying format that tracks graft status over time.


Click to show/hide R Code
#Import core demographics from "patients" file
patients_raw<-usRds::load_usrds_file("patients")%>%
  select(-ZIPCODE) #This is ZIP code at time of USRDS initiation, but we want at time of crypto dx

#Import key information about the transplants from the TX and UNOS databases
tx_raw<-usRds::load_usrds_file("tx")%>%
  select(USRDS_ID, TDATE, FAILDATE, TRR_ID_CODE)

ki_raw<-usRds::load_usrds_file("txunos_trr_ki")%>%
  select(USRDS_ID, ORGTYP, HRTX, LUTX, INTX, LITX,PITX,BMTX, TRR_ID_CODE)

kp_raw<-usRds::load_usrds_file("txunos_trr_kp")%>%
  select(USRDS_ID, ORGTYP, HRTX, LUTX, INTX, LITX,PITX,BMTX, TRR_ID_CODE)

#This combines the three datasets
tx_clean<-tx_raw%>%
  left_join(bind_rows(ki_raw,
                      kp_raw))%>%
  arrange(USRDS_ID, TDATE)%>%
  
  group_by(USRDS_ID)%>%
  mutate(cumulative_transplant_total=row_number())%>%
  ungroup

#Create a time-varying dataset that can be used to track whether a pt has an active or inactive graft and the cumulative number of txs
tx_status<-tx_clean%>%
  select(USRDS_ID, TDATE, FAILDATE, cumulative_transplant_total)%>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(TDATE, FAILDATE),
    names_to = "event_type",
    values_to = "event_date"
  ) %>%
  filter(!is.na(event_date)) %>%
  mutate(
    graft_status = case_when(
      event_type == "TDATE" ~ "Active",
      event_type == "FAILDATE" ~ "Failed"
    )
  ) %>%
  select(-event_type)%>%
  arrange(USRDS_ID, cumulative_transplant_total, event_date, graft_status)

title: Create cohort
text:
Initialize flowchart
The next component makes use of the flowchart package. This package combines two key processes in an epidemiologic analysis:

Dataset preparation: Sequential application of eligibility criteria to define the analytic cohort, with explicit tracking of excluded records at each step.
STROBE diagram preparation: STrengthening the Reporting of OBservational studies in Epidemiology diagrams visually depict the process of including/excluding patients in an observational study and grouping them into cohorts. Many journals require these as a standard Figure 1.

The code below initializes a flowchart-aware cohort object and applies sequential eligibility filters, retaining both inclusion counts and labeled exclusion steps for downstream reporting.


Click to show/hide R Code
#Initialize a flowchart cohort
patients_clean<-patients_raw%>%
  as_fc(label="Patients in USRDS")%>%
  
  
  fc_filter(TOTTX>0, 
            label="Prior transplant", 
            label_exc = "Excluded: No prior transplant", 
            show_exc = TRUE)%>%
  
  fc_filter(TX1DATE<as.Date("2021-01-01"), 
            label="Transplant prior to 2021", 
            label_exc = "Excluded: Transplant 2021 or later", 
            show_exc = TRUE)

title: Create cohort
section: Identification of comorbidities and confirmation of Medicare coverage continuity
text:
Identification of comorbidities and confirmation of Medicare coverage continuity
This component identifies baseline comorbidities among transplant recipients using diagnosis codes derived from Medicare Institutional (Part A) and physician/supplier (Part B) claims. Diagnosis code lists defined in R/setup.R are applied uniformly across claims files to establish the presence and timing of comorbid conditions.
This portion makes use of the get_IN_ICD() and get_PS_ICD() functions from the usRds package to obtain dates that specific ICD codes are used for patients with a history of at least one kidney transplant in the study period.
The establish_dx_date() function from the usRds package uses the results of this analysis to ascertain the date when each condition meets the criteria for a diagnosis. It counts a diagnosis as established on the first of:

one inpatient claim carrying a code from the condition’s list; or
a second record of any other kind carrying one: hospital outpatient, physician/supplier, skilled nursing, home health or other institutional claims.

Records are counted one at a time rather than grouped into visits, and the diagnosis date is the first day of service on the record that establishes the diagnosis. The rule, and the decision still open on it, are set out under How a case is found in claims.
In parallel, Medicare coverage history is retrieved for all transplant recipients from the payhist file, which is part of the Core dataset. These data will be used to confirm continuous enrollment during the analytic period. We verify the absence of gaps indicating missing data, noting that every subsequent period in the dataset for a patient starts the day after the previous period ends and thereby supporting valid longitudinal assessment of diagnoses and downstream cost analyses.
Finally, we separate cryptococcus diagnosis dates from other comorbidities for a separate list, given the key nature of the date of cryptococcus diagnosis for subsequent analyses.


Click to show/hide R Code
#Create list of USRDS ids for patients who have undergone transplant
transplant_id_list<-patients_clean$data%>%
  pull(USRDS_ID)

# We now seek to determine comorbidities by using diagnosis codes from the setup.R file

comorbidity_diagnosis_date<-list()

# Combine all ICD codes from all comorbidities into one list 
comorbidity_ICD_combined_list<-unlist(comorbidity_ICD_list, use.names=FALSE)

#Scrape files for any comorbidity claim
comorbidity_claims_df<-bind_rows(get_IN_ICD(icd_codes = comorbidity_ICD_combined_list, 
                                            years = 2006:2021, 
                                            usrds_ids = transplant_id_list ),
                                 get_PS_ICD(icd_codes = comorbidity_ICD_combined_list, 
                                            years = 2006:2021, 
                                            usrds_ids = transplant_id_list )%>%rename(CODE=DIAG))%>%
  arrange(USRDS_ID, CLM_FROM)

#Create comorbidity_diagnosis_date data frame
for (comorbidity in names(comorbidity_ICD_list)){
  
  comorbidity_diagnosis_date[[comorbidity]]<-comorbidity_claims_df%>%
    filter(CODE %in% comorbidity_ICD_list[[comorbidity]])%>%
    establish_dx_date(diagnosis_established = comorbidity)
}

#Load Medicare coverage history for all patients with transplant
medicare_history<-load_usrds_file("payhist",
                                  usrds_ids = transplant_id_list)%>%
  arrange(USRDS_ID, BEGDATE)%>%
  group_by(USRDS_ID)%>%
  mutate(lag_ENDDATE=lag(ENDDATE))%>%
  mutate(gap=as.numeric(BEGDATE-lag_ENDDATE))%>%
  arrange(desc(gap))

#Confirm no gaps (gap should always be 1 or missing)
if (any(!is.na(medicare_history$gap) & medicare_history$gap != 1)) {
  stop("Gap assumption violated: `gap` contains values other than 1 or NA.")
}

#Add cryptococcus diagnosis date to patients_clean$data
#First, format a df with the cryptococcus dx
cryptococcus_df<-comorbidity_diagnosis_date$cryptococcus%>%
  select(-diagnosis)%>%
  rename(cryptococcus_dx_date=date_established)

title: Create cohort
section: Further development of the STROBE flowchart
text:
Further development of the STROBE flowchart
Subsequently, key diagnosis dates, including the date of cryptococcosis diagnosis, are merged into the analytic patient dataset.
This code block then extends the STROBE flowchart by integrating diagnosis timing, eligibility criteria, and coverage requirements to finalize the analytic cohorts. Patients are classified as cryptococcosis cases or potential controls based on the presence and timing of diagnosis, and sequential exclusion criteria are applied to ensure incident disease, adult status at diagnosis, and appropriate calendar-time eligibility.
The verify_medicare_primary() function from the usRds package is used to confirm that patients with a cryptococcus diagnosis have Medicare primary coverage for at least 365 days prior to the cryptococcus diagnosis date, so that a diagnosis established earlier in that year would have been seen. This makes it more likely that the diagnosis is new, but does not prove it (What a claims-based definition can and cannot show).
These steps culminate in the final case and control cohorts, with all inclusion and exclusion decisions explicitly tracked and visualized in the updated STROBE flow diagram.


Click to show/hide R Code
#Join cryptococcus date to fc cohort
patients_clean$data<-left_join(patients_clean$data, 
                               cryptococcus_df)%>%
  mutate(cryptococcus_case=ifelse(is.na(cryptococcus_dx_date), "Potential control", "Case"))

#Continue to create analytic cohort
patients_merged<-patients_clean%>%
  
  #Remove patients with a diagnosis of cryptococcus prior to transplant
  fc_filter(cryptococcus_dx_date>TX1DATE | is.na(cryptococcus_dx_date), 
            label="No cryptococcus dx prior to transplant", 
            label_exc = "Excluded: cryptococcus dx prior to transplant", 
            show_exc = TRUE)%>%
  
  fc_filter((time_length(interval(BORN, cryptococcus_dx_date), "years") >= 18) | is.na(cryptococcus_dx_date),
            label="Age 18+ at time of cryptococcus if cryptococcus patient", 
            label_exc = "Excluded: First cryptococcus prior to age 18", 
            show_exc = TRUE)%>%
  
  fc_filter((year(cryptococcus_dx_date)>=2007 & year(cryptococcus_dx_date)<=2020) | is.na(cryptococcus_dx_date),
            label="Incident cryptococcus between 1/1/2007 and 12/31/2020", 
            label_exc = "Incident cryptococcus outside of specified date range", 
            show_exc = TRUE)%>%
  
  #Split cohorts
  fc_split(cryptococcus_case)
  
  #Check Medicare coverage for 365-day lookback period from day of first episode of cryptococcus
patients_merged$data<-patients_merged$data%>%
  verify_medicare_primary(index_date = "cryptococcus_dx_date",
                          lookback_days = 365,
                          coverage_start_variable = "coverage_start_date",
                          coverage_end_variable = "coverage_end_date"
                          )%>%
  mutate(medicare_primary_TF=ifelse(cryptococcus_case=="Potential control", TRUE, medicare_primary_TF))
  
patients_merged2<-patients_merged%>%
  
  fc_filter(medicare_primary_TF==TRUE, 
            label = "365+ days of Medicare primary coverage\nprior to first cryptococcus claim", 
            label_exc = "Excluded: Fewer than 365 days of coverage",
            show_exc = TRUE)

patients_merged2$data<-patients_merged2$data%>%
  select(-medicare_primary_TF)%>%
  
  #Prepare data for cohort initialization
  mutate(terminal_date=coalesce(coverage_end_date, censor_date))

patients_merged2<-patients_merged2%>%
  fc_filter((terminal_date - cryptococcus_dx_date >=minimum_followup) | is.na(cryptococcus_dx_date), 
            label = "Minimum followup exceeded", 
            label_exc= "Excluded: Minimum follow-up threshold not met",
            show_exc = TRUE)

  
patients_merged2%>%
  fc_draw()

text:
Creation of a time-varying cohort
We use several functions from the usRds package:

create_usrds_cohort()
add_cohort_covariate()

title: Analysis and reporting
text:
Statistical analysis

The primary model
Why the model describes mean cost directly is explained under Why cost data are hard to model. Each person-month’s cost is modelled with a generalized linear model that has:

a log link and a Tweedie distribution;
terms for group (case or control), month (as a category) and their interaction, so that the difference between cases and controls can differ in every month;
the logarithm of the number of days observed as an offset.

What each of these does is explained under Models for costs. Standard errors come from generalized estimating equations clustered on matched set, and also on patient if one person can appear in more than one matched set.
Specified in: §8.4 Primary model.


From the model to a dollar estimate

For each month, the model predicts the mean cost of a full 30-day month for cases and for controls.
The case-minus-control difference is taken for each month.
The differences for months 0 to 11 are added up. That total is the excess cost per case.
A 95% confidence interval comes from a cluster bootstrap: matched sets are resampled with replacement 1,000 times (or more if needed), and the whole calculation is repeated each time.

The same model gives the month-by-month profile of excess cost from month −3 to month 11, and fitting it separately to each care setting (inpatient, outpatient, skilled nursing, home health, hospice, dialysis, physician/supplier) divides the excess by setting.
Specified in: §8.4 Primary model, §8.5 Secondary analyses.

Decision pending: whether the estimate relies on matching alone, with months −3 to −1 reported as a balance check, or subtracts the difference between cases and controls before diagnosis as well, which gives a difference-in-differences estimate (D9).



What the code does now
The code fits five models to each of ten monthly cost outcomes: total cost, institutional cost, physician/supplier cost, and seven institutional categories (inpatient, outpatient, skilled nursing, home health, hospice, dialysis, and a non-claim/auxiliary category). None is yet the primary model as specified, and the total currently reported is not yet the planned estimate.

Known differences from the plan:

the reported total adds up each month’s case–control difference measured relative to month −3, including months −2 and −1, so it is not the sum of differences over months 0 to 11 (#2);
the models on the dollar and log(cost + 1) scales include the days-observed offset in a way that only makes sense with a log link (#4);
the calculation for log-link models adds ratios rather than dollar differences (#5);
plots label back-transformed predictions from the log(cost + 1) and mixed models as mean dollars (#14);
the identifier of each matched set is not carried into the modelling data, so models can cluster only on patient (see also #12);
the cluster bootstrap is not yet implemented.



Missing covariate data
Cost is observed only during covered months, by design. For covariates from the registry, missingness is described, and if it exceeds 5% for any covariate in a propensity score, multiple imputation by chained equations is used.
Specified in: §8.6 Missing data.

Plotting mean monthly costs
plot_mean_monthly_costs()
The following function uses ggplot2 to create a plot of monthly costs with a risk table underneath.
Its inputs are as follows:

fitted_model: the fit object from models created in the R/modeling.R script
countdf: a data frame containing the appropriate count data for cases and controls at each time point, used to create a risk table

The function uses the emmeans function from the package of the same name to estimate monthly costs. The x-axis (months) is shifted to the right so that the vertical line at x=0 cleanly separates pre-index and post-index months, and cases and controls are dodged slightly so that the error bars do not overlap.
Used in the analysis: Figures: Month-by-month plots.


Click to show/hide R Code
#Function that returns a ggplot of the mean cost (with confidence interval) for cryptococcus cases and controls by month
plot_mean_monthly_costs<-function(fitted_model, countdf=final_count_df) {

  #First, use emmeans to calculate the predicted values from the model assuming 30-day months, then convert to data frame
  emm_df <- emmeans(
    fitted_model,
    ~ patient_type | month,
    at = list(month_offset = 30),
    type = "response"
  )%>%as.data.frame()%>%
    
    #Shifts all points and error_bars 0.5 to the right to avoid the zero-line
    mutate(month=0.5+as.numeric(month))%>%
    
    #Move cases 0.1 to the right and controls 0.1 to the left to improve legibility
  mutate(month=ifelse(patient_type=="Case", month+0.1, month-0.1))%>%
    mutate(
      estimate = if ("response" %in% names(.)) response else emmean)
  
  monthly_plot <- list()
  
  # Main plot
  monthly_plot[["main"]] <- ggplot(data = emm_df) +
    geom_point(aes(x = month, y = estimate, color = patient_type)) +
    geom_errorbar(
      aes(
        x = month,
        ymin = asymp.LCL,
        ymax = asymp.UCL,
        color = patient_type
      ),
      width = 0.1
    ) +
    geom_vline(xintercept = 0,
               linetype = "dashed",
               color = "gray50") +
    theme_classic() +
    labs(
      x = "Month",
      y = "Inflation-adjusted cost per month (dollars)",
      color = "Patient group"
    )+
    theme(legend.position = "bottom")
  
  # Risk table
  monthly_plot[["risk_table"]] <- countdf %>%
    mutate(month = 0.5 + as.numeric(month),
           y_position = ifelse(patient_type == "Case", 0.4, 0.6)) %>%
    ggplot() +
    geom_text(
      aes(x = month, y = y_position, label = n, color=patient_type),
      size = 3
    )+
    coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0.3, 0.7)) +
    theme_void() +
    theme(
      plot.margin = margin(t = -5, b = 5),
      legend.position = "none")
  
  # Combine plots
  monthly_plot[["main"]] /
    monthly_plot[["risk_table"]] +
    plot_layout(heights = c(9, 1), guides = "keep")+
    plot_annotation(
      caption = "Bottom panel shows N at risk by month"
    )
  
}

The following function is passed a control df and a number of values for a case patient, and returns the number of distinct controls which are potential matches. The matching algorithm is hard-coded.

#Function that defines the number of potential control matches for a case
calculate_number_potential_matches<-function(control_df,
                                             USRDS_ID,
                                             birthdate,
                                             cirrhosis_status,
                                             cmv_status,
                                             hiv_status,
                                             diabetes_status,
                                             matching_date,
                                             matching_days_since_transplant) {
  
  print(paste0("Calculating number of potential controls for patient: ", USRDS_ID))
  control_df%>%
    
    #Exact match on cirrhosis, CMV, HIV, and diabetes status
    filter(cirrhosis==cirrhosis_status)%>%
    #  filter(CMV==cmv_status)%>%
    filter(HIV==hiv_status)%>%
    filter(diabetes==diabetes_status)%>%
    
    #Risk set matching
    filter(tstart<=matching_days_since_transplant)%>%
    filter(tstop>matching_days_since_transplant)%>%
    
    #Calculate date for age calculations/etc.
    mutate(.baseline_control_date=matching_days_since_transplant+most_recent_transplant_date)%>%
    
    #Make sure case and control are sampled within 3 years of each other
    filter(abs(time_length(interval(.baseline_control_date, matching_date), "years")) <=3)%>%
    
    #Date matching
    #  filter(cohort_start_date<=matching_date)%>%
    #  filter(cohort_stop_date>matching_date)%>%
    
    #Age>=18 on index date
    filter(time_length(interval(BORN, .baseline_control_date), "years") >= 18)%>%
    
    #Age difference under 10 years, calculated at sampling date
    filter(abs(time_length(interval(BORN,.baseline_control_date), "years")-
                 time_length(interval(birthdate,matching_date), "years")) <=10)%>%
    
    #Confirming 365 day Medicare lookback available for potential match
    verify_medicare_primary(index_date = matching_date, medicare_coverage_df = medicare_history, cache=TRUE)%>%
    filter(medicare_primary_TF==TRUE)%>%
    
    #Count rows after ensuring controls with mult transplants are only counted once 
    distinct(USRDS_ID)%>%
    nrow()%>%
    return()
  
}

Total excess costs
calculate_total_excess_costs()
This function takes a fit object from a model and calculates the total estimated excess costs and confidence intervals. This object currently only works for models with linear links.
Used in the analysis: Tables: Modeled total excess costs.


Click to show/hide R Code
# Calculate total excess costs in a model
calculate_total_excess_costs <- function(fitted_model, link = "linear") {
  
  # Extract coefficients and vcov matrix
  coef_df <- tidy(fitted_model)
  vcov_matrix <- vcov(fitted_model)
  
  # Get interaction terms
  interaction_names <- coef_df %>% 
    filter(str_detect(term, ":")) %>% 
    pull(term)
  
  if (link == "linear") {
    # Sum of coefficients
    sum_estimate <- coef_df %>% 
      filter(term %in% interaction_names) %>% 
      pull(estimate) %>% 
      sum()
    
    # Variance of sum
    sum_variance <- vcov_matrix[interaction_names, interaction_names] %>% 
      sum()
    
    # Standard error and CI
    sum_se <- sqrt(sum_variance)
    df <- df.residual(fitted_model)
    
    tibble(
      estimate = sum_estimate,
      std_error = sum_se,
      conf_low = estimate - qt(0.975, df) * std_error,
      conf_high = estimate + qt(0.975, df) * std_error,
      statistic = estimate / std_error,
      p_value = 2 * pt(-abs(statistic), df)
    )
    
  } else if (link == "log") {
    # Get coefficients for interactions
    coefs <- coef(fitted_model)[interaction_names]
    vcov_sub <- vcov_matrix[interaction_names, interaction_names]
    
    # Exponentiate each coefficient
    exp_coefs <- exp(coefs)
    
    # Sum of exponentiated coefficients
    sum_estimate <- sum(exp_coefs)
    
    # Delta method for variance
    # Gradient: derivative of sum(exp(beta)) w.r.t. each beta is exp(beta)
    gradient <- exp_coefs
    
    # Variance using delta method
    sum_variance <- as.numeric(t(gradient) %*% vcov_sub %*% gradient)
    sum_se <- sqrt(sum_variance)
    
    # CI using normal approximation (GLM)
    tibble(
      estimate = sum_estimate,
      std_error = sum_se,
      conf_low = estimate - qnorm(0.975) * std_error,
      conf_high = estimate + qnorm(0.975) * std_error,
      statistic = estimate / std_error,
      p_value = 2 * pnorm(-abs(statistic))
    )
    
  } else {
    stop("link must be either 'linear' or 'log'")
  }
}

The project
This repository estimates the excess Medicare payments attributable to cryptococcosis after kidney transplant. It uses United States Renal Data System (USRDS) data, which link OPTN/UNOS transplant records to Medicare claims, and it publishes its code and methods as a Quarto website.

analysis-plan.md is the source of truth for design. It covers the cohort, exposure, time zero, matching, cost construction, estimands, models, and sensitivity analyses. Code implements the plan; it does not redefine it.

If the code needs to depart from the plan, change the plan in the same pull request.
Plan changes are tracked in git, not in a change log inside the plan. Commit each design change on its own, with a message that gives the reason and says whether any results that depend on it had already been seen.
The plan lists open design choices as Decision Dn in its “Open decisions” table. Do not settle one in code. Raise it with the maintainer.

This is an analysis project, not an R package, even though the scripts live in R/ and there is an .Rbuildignore. Do not add DESCRIPTION, NAMESPACE, roxygen, or pkgdown infrastructure. Do not apply CRAN conventions.
Implementation status lives in GitHub Issues, not in these files. When you find a gap between the code and the plan, or a defect, open or update an issue. Reference the issue in the pull request that closes it.

R scripts

Running the analysis. Open the .Rproj and run R/main.R from the project root. main.R sources the other scripts in dependency order. ARCHITECTURE.md describes what each script does and how data flows between them.
One job per script: setup, cohort construction, matching, cost processing, modeling, tables, figures. When you add a script:

source it from main.R at the right point
update ARCHITECTURE.md in the same commit

Header comment. Each script begins with a comment saying what it does and which objects it needs from earlier scripts.
Constants, libraries, and code lists live in R/setup.R. Other scripts do not call library(), re-source setup.R, or hard-code values. Any number a reader might want to change, such as a window length, a year, a caliper, or the matching ratio, is a named constant in setup.R.
Helper functions go in R/functions.R, sourced after setup.R. A function takes its inputs as arguments and does not read global objects, including through default arguments.
No side effects outside the project. Do not use setwd(), absolute paths, or writes outside the project. Locate data only through usRds’s set_USRDS_wd().
Exploration code does not stay in pipeline scripts. Delete it, or move it below a chunk label that no Quarto page uses. The website shows the scripts as they are.
Deprecated scripts. R/define_cohort.R is deprecated (it uses strobe) and is not sourced. Do not build on it; R/create_cohort.R is the active script.

Chunk labels
Scripts are divided into labelled sections, so that Quarto pages can show the code without copying it:
## ---- merge-costs

Every logical step has a label. A label covers the code from its line to the next label.
Labels are kebab-case, describe the step, and are unique across all scripts. Quarto pulls chunks by label, so a duplicate label silently picks up the wrong code.
Renaming or deleting a label breaks the Quarto page that uses it. Search the .qmd files before you change one.
Scripts must still run end to end through main.R. Labels are comments and must never change what the code does.

Variable labels

Label analysis variables with human-readable descriptions, for example with labelled::set_variable_labels(). Tables then show readable names without renaming code by hand.
For USRDS variables, use usRds’s apply_usrds_varlabels() and apply_usrds_factors() rather than writing labels by hand.
Label each derived variable where it is created. Include units, the price year for costs, and windows where they apply (for example, “Medicare payments, month 0, January 2021 dollars”).

Quarto website
The Quarto site documents the code. It does not run the analysis.

Setup files: _quarto.yml, index.qmd and 404.qmd (the page GitHub Pages shows for a missing address) sit at the root. There is one page per pipeline script in quarto/, named after the script (for example, quarto/create_cohort.qmd for R/create_cohort.R). quarto/results.qmd is a placeholder for results and says they are pending. The custom-callout extension in _extensions/ provides the Rcode, Results and Pending callouts, and the issue-comments extension lets readers highlight text and leave a comment, which a relay files as a GitHub issue in this repository.
Showing code: each page loads its script with knitr::read_chunk("../R/<script>.R") in a hidden chunk. It then shows each labelled section in a chunk with #| eval: false, with prose explaining what the section does and why. Pages link to the script on GitHub and to the scripts it depends on.

The render: list in _quarto.yml keeps Quarto from also rendering the root files as pages of their own. Two adjustments keep links and diagrams working on both GitHub and the site:

The plan page uses GitHub-style heading IDs (from: markdown+gfm_auto_identifiers), so links such as #13-open-decisions resolve.
The Architecture page reads ARCHITECTURE.md as text and marks its ```mermaid diagrams as Quarto diagrams. It reads only that file. Write diagrams in ARCHITECTURE.md with plain ```mermaid fences.

Rendering: the site renders to docs/, which is not committed. .github/workflows/publish.yml renders it on every pull request as a check and, on each push to master, publishes it to the gh-pages branch, which GitHub Pages serves. Render locally to preview a change to a script’s labels or a page’s prose, but do not commit the output.
New scripts: when you add a script, add its page and its sidebar entry in _quarto.yml in the same commit.
Prose must match the code. If a change alters what a section does, update that section’s explanation in the same pull request.

Outputs

Exported files: tables and figures are exported by R/tables.R and R/figures.R to tables/ and figures/. Both folders are gitignored, because their contents are results under the disclosure rules below.
Figures need alt text when they are published.
README.Rmd is the source of README.md. Edit the .Rmd and re-knit; do not edit README.md directly.

Restricted data (applies to everyone)
USRDS and Medicare data are covered by a data use agreement (DUA). The rules below apply to people and agents alike.

Never commit data. That includes USRDS files, extracts, and any saved R object or output derived from patient-level data (.rds, .RData, .parquet, .csv, and the like). Keep data outside the repository, and check .gitignore before adding a new output type.
AI agents must not read restricted data. Anything an agent opens, prints, or summarizes is sent to the model provider. Agents therefore must not:

open data files or patient-level objects
print rows or head() of them
display USRDS IDs, person-level dates, ZIP codes, or individual cost records

This applies unless your own DUA explicitly permits that use. Agents may write code, review it, and run it on synthetic data that mimics the column names and types. Results on real data are produced by an authorized person.
Use synthetic data for development and tests. Build small synthetic data frames in code, label them clearly as synthetic, and never derive them from real records.
Disclosure. No table, figure, flowchart box, or text may show a count from 1 to 10. That includes counts that can be recovered by subtraction or from complementary cells, and counts in risk tables under plots. Figures that plot individual people (beeswarm, scatter) are not published. Check every output before it leaves the secure environment, and check the exact wording of the governing DUA before dissemination.

Look in usRds first
The usRds package is the first place to look for anything that touches USRDS files: loading files, extracting claims, diagnosis dates, Medicare coverage, cohort helpers, costs, proration, and inflation adjustment.

Check the package’s function reference before writing project-specific code. Use an existing function, or extend it.
Package problems belong in the package. If a usRds function is wrong, or does almost but not exactly what the plan needs, open an issue in the usRds repository rather than documenting it here. Then do one of two things:

fix it in usRds, which is preferred when the behavior is generally useful
wrap it in this project, with a code comment that links the issue

Remove the wrapper when the issue is fixed.
Before relying on a function’s behavior, read its documentation and its open issues. This matters most for verify_medicare_primary(), establish_dx_date(), prorate_costs_by_day(), and adjust_costs_for_inflation(), whose behavior directly sets the cohort and the cost outcome.
Record the usRds version (or commit) used for any result.

USRDS data facts
Sources: USRDS 2025 Researcher’s Guide, Appendix B (data file descriptions), and Appendix C (formats). Check these against the release you are using.
Institutional (“IN”) claims cover more than inpatient care. They include inpatient, outpatient, skilled nursing facility (SNF), home health, and hospice claims.

HCFASAF gives the claim type: I inpatient, O outpatient, N SNF, H home health, S hospice. In older files, M is a REBUS inpatient stay.
From 2002 on, each type has its own files: ip_*, op_*, sn_*, hh_*, and hs_*, each with a CLM (claim), DXP (diagnosis/procedure), and DET (revenue center) file.
Institutional claims are uniquely identified by USRDS_ID, CLM_FROM, and SEQ_KEYC.

Physician/supplier (PS) claims come as a CLM (claim), LINE (line item), and DX (diagnosis) file.

Each line carries one diagnosis and one procedure code.
One visit produces several lines, so lines must be grouped into encounters for counts of visits.
Be explicit about whether you use line-level or claim-level amounts and diagnoses.

Payment and charge fields. The cost outcome uses Medicare payments, never charges.








File
Medicare payment
Charges (do not use as cost)




Institutional claim (*_CLM)
CLM_AMT
CLM_TOT


Institutional revenue center (*_DET)
REVPMT
REV_CH


Physician/supplier claim (PS_CLM)
CLM_PMT_AMT
NCH_CARR_SBMT_CHRG_AMT (submitted), NCH_CARR_ALOW_CHRG_AMT (allowed)


Physician/supplier line
PMTAMT
SBMTCH (submitted), ALOWCH (allowed)




IP_DET and SN_DET have no REVPMT. Revenue-center payments exist only for outpatient, home health, and hospice lines, so revenue-center payment totals do not include inpatient or SNF care.
Summed REVPMT for an outpatient claim does not always equal that claim’s CLM_AMT (about 3% higher overall). Never add institutional claim payments and revenue-center payments together; they describe the same services.
Revenue center code 0001 is the sum of a claim’s other revenue-center charges. Exclude it when summing revenue-center lines.
Inpatient CLM_AMT excludes CMS pass-through payments (indirect medical education, capital, kidney acquisition). The pass-through amount is PER_DIEM × CVR_DCNT. Whether to include it is a design choice for the plan.
From the 2015 files on, PRPAYAMT (primary payer paid amount) and TDEDAMT (beneficiary deductible and coinsurance) are also available.

Claims year. Claims are assigned to a SAF year by the service end date, not the start date.
Data currency (2025 release).

Claims are complete through 2023-12-31, except for the Q1 2024 inpatient file.
The core files, including deaths, run through 2024-12-31.
Vital status runs ahead of claims by about a year.

Payer history (payhist)

Eligible Medicare fee-for-service primary coverage: PAYER is MPAB or MPO. This is the Researcher’s Guide definition (Example 8), and claims are complete only for these periods.
Not eligible: HMO (Medicare Advantage), MSP-EGHP, MSP-nonEGHP, OTH, WAIT.
A month without eligible coverage is unobserved, not zero cost. Code must never turn missing claims during uncovered time into zeros.
Medicare entitlement based only on ESRD ends three years after a successful transplant. Expect coverage loss after that point.

ICD transition. ICD-9-CM applies to services before 2015-10-01. ICD-10-CM and ICD-10-PCS apply on or after that date.

Codes are stored without periods.
Decide, and document, which date sets the code system for a hospital stay that crosses the transition.

Unclear variables. If a variable’s meaning is unclear, check Appendix B and Appendix C. Do not guess from the name.

Coding conventions

Flowchart labels and text are built from the constants in setup.R, not hard-coded. For example, a label that says “2007-2020” or “365+ days” goes stale when the constants change.
Code lists

Each code carries its category, its ICD version or code type (diagnosis or procedure), and its matching rule (exact or prefix).
Each code belongs to exactly one category.
Check every code against the official CMS ICD-9-CM, ICD-10-CM, ICD-10-PCS, and HCPCS code sets.
Never invent codes, variables, files, or clinical definitions.

Cohort flow uses the flowchart package (as_fc(), fc_filter(), fc_split(), fc_draw()). Every inclusion or exclusion goes through fc_filter(). Never drop rows from $data outside the flowchart; the diagram must reproduce the cohort exactly. The cohort used downstream is the data from the final flowchart step.
Matching

Matching must be reproducible from a recorded seed. Control selection must not depend on row order.
The matched-set identifier is kept as an ordinary column through to the modeling data, so models and bootstraps can cluster on it.
Report the number of cases with each number of matched controls, including zero.

Costs

Each person-month records both its cost and its number of observed days, so partial months are explicit.
Every cost carries its price year. Inflation adjustment uses the constants in setup.R.
Floors, caps, or other changes to cost values (for example, setting negative months to zero) are design choices. They belong in the plan before they go in code.

Joins

Use join_by() with an explicit relationship where you can.
After every interval join (between(), closest(), overlaps()) and every join of claims to people, assert that it did not multiply rows.
Decide deliberately what happens to people with no match (NA rows): keep them, exclude them through a flowchart step, or stop with an error.

Dates and windows

Write windows as inclusive day offsets from time zero, matching the plan (for example, month 0 is days 0 to 29).
Test the window edges on synthetic data.

Models. Keep the code that turns model coefficients into reported dollars (contrasts, retransformation, sums over months) in named functions in R/functions.R, and test them on synthetic data with a known answer.
Style: the tidyverse style guide. Style changes go in their own commits, separate from changes that alter analytical behavior.

Checks for any change
Before opening a pull request, check the items below that apply to your change.
Cohort construction

Do the order, the denominator, and the labels of each flowchart step match the condition it applies?
Can each count be reproduced from the code?
Is the downstream cohort the data from the final flowchart step?

Exposure and time zero

Which claim files, claim types (HCFASAF), diagnosis positions, and date fields define cryptococcosis?
Is matching exact or prefix, and are both ICD-9 and ICD-10 covered for the right dates?
Is time zero defined as in the plan for cases and for controls?
Is every covariate measured using only information from before time zero?

Matching

Are controls at risk and undiagnosed at the case’s time since transplant?
Does control eligibility use only information available at that time, with no conditioning on future events?
Is selection reproducible from the seed, and independent of row order?
Are unmatched and partially matched cases counted and reported?

Coverage and follow-up

Does Medicare coverage span the whole look-back window, not just its start?
Are adjacent coverage spans merged without allowing uncovered days?
Does follow-up end at every event the plan lists (death, loss of coverage, maximum follow-up, administrative end)?

Costs

Are payment fields used, not charge fields?
Is any service counted twice (claim plus revenue-center amounts, or revenue code 0001)?
Are uncovered months excluded rather than recorded as zero?
Are claims assigned to the right month around time zero, including multi-day claims?

Models and reported numbers

Does the reported estimate match the estimand in the plan (which months, which scale, which contrast)?
Do standard errors account for clustering as the plan specifies?
Do the tables, figures, and website prose say what the model actually estimates?

Structure and documentation

Does ARCHITECTURE.md still describe the scripts and the data flow?
Are the chunk labels unique, and does each script’s Quarto page still find every label it uses?
Does every script have a Quarto page and a sidebar entry, and does the pull request’s render check pass?
Are all site chunks eval: false, apart from the Setup page’s constants and icd-code-lists sections and their summary tables, and the Architecture page’s chunk that reads ARCHITECTURE.md?
Does Rscript tests/check-crosslinks.R check pass?
Are new derived variables labelled?

Execution

Does main.R run from a clean session (Ctrl+Shift+F10 in RStudio, then source main.R), with no objects left over from earlier work?
Are paths relative, with no hard-coded data directories? Use set_USRDS_wd().
Are package versions recorded?
Are any saved intermediates stale?

Validation on real data (run by an authorized person; report only aggregate, suppressed results)

row counts before and after each join of claims to people
the number of cases with 2, 1, and 0 matched controls
standardized mean differences at time zero, including cost in months −3 to −1
person-months by group and coverage status, and person-months after death
case counts by ICD-9 versus ICD-10 era

Working with agents

Autonomy. The person directing an agent decides how much it may do. That person may also give the agent stricter rules of their own, and those take precedence over this section. By default, an agent may:

edit code and documentation
add scripts and tests
run code and render the site on synthetic data
commit to a branch and open a pull request

Collaborators: master is protected. Changes reach it only through a pull request that the maintainer reviews.
Every agent, under any level of autonomy:

follows the restricted-data rules above
asks before any step that would read real data, run the full pipeline, or make expensive calls
does not settle an open decision in the plan

Keep pull requests focused. In each one, state which section of the plan or which issue it addresses, and what was checked. Say whether it was checked on synthetic data or by reading only. Never describe synthetic results as results.
For references, use the USRDS Researcher’s Guide and its appendices, the CMS code sets, and PubMed. Cite what you used: add a verified entry (with its DOI or PMID, or the official URL and release) to references.bib and cite it as [@key] in the plan and on site pages, not as a bare link.
Project documentsRepository blueprint Code

Analytical scripts

R/main.R sources definitive scripts in dependency order.
Typical workflow: setup → cohort construction → processing → modeling → outputs.
Study-specific scripts may be grouped into subdirectories by analytical stage.
R/tables.R and R/figures.R may generate outputs directly or orchestrate specialized scripts.

Documentation

Document definitive analytical scripts with explanatory Quarto pages; exploratory scripts need not have pages.
Use Cryptococcus-cost-analysis as an example for Quarto supporting files, chunk imports, callouts, and formatting—not scientific methods.
Quarto source and rendered output locations may vary by project.

Outputs and version control

Track approved, nonrestricted outputs when useful for publication; otherwise retain them locally and exclude them from Git.
.gitignore: Exclude restricted data, credentials, caches, temporary files, and generated outputs unless intentionally tracked (e.g., .Rproj.user/, .Rhistory, .RData, .httr-oauth, .quarto/, cache/, figures/, tables/, *.quarto_ipynb); verify exclusions cover actual output paths without hiding necessary source or reference files.

title: Overview
text:
The study question
This study estimates the excess Medicare payments in the 12 months after cryptococcosis is diagnosed among adult kidney transplant recipients, compared with similar recipients at the same time since transplant who have not been diagnosed.

Population: adult kidney transplant recipients in the United States with fee-for-service Medicare as their primary payer.
Comparison: each case is compared with up to two recipients who have reached the same time since transplant without being diagnosed.
Outcome: Medicare payments, month by month, from three months before diagnosis to the end of the twelfth month after it.
Measure: the average excess payment per case over the 12 months after diagnosis.


Decision pending: whether other payer arrangements, such as Medicare as secondary payer, are ever eligible (D1).

The data come from the United States Renal Data System (USRDS), which links transplant registry records to Medicare claims1.

title: Overview
text:
Why it matters
Cryptococcosis is uncommon after kidney transplant2,3, but it is serious: in a national USRDS cohort, 22% of kidney recipients hospitalized for it died within six months4. Treatment of cryptococcal meningitis lasts at least 10 weeks5. Published US cost estimates are of single hospital stays, of modelled treatment, or of costs over time without a comparison group. We found no study that estimates the excess Medicare payments attributable to cryptococcosis over the months after diagnosis in kidney transplant recipients. Clinical background sets out the evidence.

title: Overview
text:
Study timeline and cost trajectories
Figure 1 illustrates how the planned study windows relate to case and control costs. The 365-day eligibility lookback is longer than the monthly cost-outcome window. Disease-related care and diagnostic workup can raise costs before the recorded diagnosis, so the prediagnosis trajectory is part of what the study aims to describe.






Figure 1: Conceptual study timeframes and mean cost trajectories; no patient data or study estimates are shown. The monthly outcome panel spans days −90 to 359. Earlier dashed curves provide context outside that panel. Shaded differences are illustrative and do not establish causal attribution.



Open the figure at full size.
For cases, time zero is the first qualifying diagnosis claim; controls are aligned at the same time since their most recent transplant, so their calendar dates may differ. The figure explains the intended windows, not the completeness of observation: coverage loss, death, and partial months require the handling specified in the analysis plan. Earlier costs may also inform planned matching covariates; they are outside the monthly outcome panel shown here.

title: Overview
text:
Methods
Each patient diagnosed with cryptococcosis (a case) is compared with up to two similar recipients who have reached the same time since transplant without being diagnosed (controls). Cases and controls are followed for 12 months from the same starting point, and the difference in their Medicare payments is the excess cost of cryptococcosis.
The Study design and methods pages set out who is studied, how cases are found, how controls are matched, how costs are built and how they are analysed, with what the plan specifies and where the code stands.

title: Study overview
section: The question and the design in brief
text:
The question and the design in brief
Question. Among adult kidney transplant recipients, how much more does Medicare pay for a patient’s care in the 12 months after cryptococcosis is diagnosed than it would have paid had they not developed it?
Approach. Each patient diagnosed with cryptococcosis (a case) is compared with up to two similar recipients who have reached the same time since transplant without being diagnosed (controls). Cases and controls are followed for 12 months from the same starting point, and the difference in their Medicare payments is the excess cost of cryptococcosis.
What is estimated. The average excess cost among people who develop cryptococcosis (the average treatment effect in the treated, or ATT): the mean difference in total Medicare payments over months 0 to 11 between cases and their matched controls, per case.
Specified in: §1 Objective, §2 Design, §8.3 Estimand.

title: Study overview
text:
Data used
The data come from the United States Renal Data System and its linked Medicare claims, described on Methodological background. This study uses the patient, transplant, payer history, treatment history and death files, and Medicare Part A and Part B claims. Part D prescription records are planned only where a covariate needs them. Claims from 2006 to 2021 are used, cases are diagnosed between 2007 and 2020, and follow-up ends on 1 January 2022. The data are used under a data use agreement and are not published.
Both institutional and physician/supplier claims are used (Medicare claims). Because claims are complete only under fee-for-service primary coverage (Medicare as primary payer), a person is observed only during periods when fee-for-service Medicare is their primary payer for both Part A and Part B, as recorded in the USRDS payer history file. Many kidney transplant recipients lose Medicare coverage over time: Medicare entitlement based only on kidney failure ends 36 months after a successful transplant, unless the person qualifies another way (for example by age or disability). The study’s findings therefore apply to recipients with fee-for-service Medicare as their primary payer.
Specified in: §3 Data source, §4.2 Eligibility, §11 Limitations.
Current code: two payer history categories count as coverage: “Medicare fee-for-service primary pay, for both Part A and Part B” and “Medicare fee-for-service primary pay, for other”. This follows the USRDS Researcher’s Guide definition of Medicare as primary payer. The guide does not say which Medicare parts the second category covers.

Decision pending: whether other payer arrangements, such as Medicare as secondary payer, are ever eligible (D1).

title: Study overview
text:
Who is studied
The source population is kidney transplant recipients in USRDS with a transplant before 2021. Cases and controls must meet the same criteria at their own time zero (defined under Time zero). A person is eligible if they:

have had at least one kidney transplant before that date;
are aged 18 or older;
have no earlier cryptococcosis diagnosis;
have had fee-for-service Medicare as primary payer for Parts A and B for the whole 365 days before that date, without gaps, so that their baseline health and baseline cost are fully observed;
are alive and under observation on that date.

The time scale is time since the most recent kidney transplant. People with more than one transplant are eligible, and their earlier transplants are counted as a covariate.
Specified in: §4 Study population.
Current code:

The 365-day coverage window is counted back from time zero, and it can begin before the transplant, for example in a recipient covered by Medicare during dialysis. The plan does not say whether the window must fall after transplant.
Recipients of a kidney–pancreas transplant are included. A pancreas transplant flag taken from diagnosis codes is described in the baseline table, but the transplant records are not used to identify these recipients, and the flag is not used in matching or the models.
A diagnosis on the day of the first transplant is treated as a diagnosis before transplant, and the patient is excluded.


Decision pending: whether kidney–pancreas and other multi-organ recipients are excluded or included with an indicator (D2).

Identifying cryptococcosis and time zero

How a case is found in claims
Cryptococcosis is identified from diagnosis codes on Medicare claims: ICD-9-CM codes for services before 1 October 2015 and ICD-10-CM codes from that date on. The code list is shown on the Setup page.
The current rule counts a diagnosis as established on the first of:

one inpatient claim carrying a cryptococcosis code; or
a second record of any other kind carrying a code: hospital outpatient, physician/supplier, skilled nursing, home health or other institutional claims.

A code in any diagnosis position counts. There is no time limit between the two records, and two on the same day count as two. Records are counted one at a time rather than grouped into visits, so a single outpatient visit that lists the code more than once may be enough. The diagnosis date is the first day of service on the record that establishes the diagnosis.
Specified in: §5.1 Exposure definition (the code list), §5.2 Diagnosis date. The plan gives the diagnosis date as the service date of the “first qualifying claim”. Under a two-claim rule that could mean the first coded claim or the one that completes the rule; the code uses the second.

Decision pending: the claim algorithm, meaning which claim types and diagnosis positions count, how many claims are needed and within what window (D3). The rule above is what the code does now.



What a claims-based definition can and cannot show
A claim shows that a clinician recorded the diagnosis for billing. It does not show that the infection was confirmed by culture, antigen testing or histopathology, and codes are sometimes recorded while a diagnosis is being ruled out. Some cases will therefore be misclassified (Finding a diagnosis in claims).
The 365-day window of complete coverage before diagnosis means that, had the rule been met earlier in that year, it would have been seen. An earlier single record carrying the code can still fall inside the window: when the diagnosis is established by a second record, the first always comes before it. Complete coverage makes it more likely the diagnosis is new, but it does not prove the infection began then. A person with a diagnosis before their first transplant is excluded.
Two planned sensitivity analyses address this: a stricter claims definition, and separate analyses of diagnoses before and after the October 2015 change from ICD-9-CM to ICD-10-CM (§9).


Time zero
Time zero is the day from which costs are counted, and before which everything used for matching or adjustment is measured.

Cases: the diagnosis date.
Controls: the day on which the control reaches the same number of days since their own most recent transplant as the case had at diagnosis.

For example, if a case is diagnosed 243 days after their transplant, each of their controls has time zero 243 days after the control’s own transplant. That is usually a different calendar date from the case’s. The study timeline on the home page shows how time zero, the eligibility lookback and the monthly cost windows fit together.
Specified in: §5.3 Time zero.

title: Cases and controls
text:
Choosing comparison patients

Risk-set matching
Controls are chosen by risk-set matching (Risk-set matching). For each case, the risk set is everyone who, at the case’s time since transplant, is still eligible and has not been diagnosed.
Two reasons make time since transplant the right time scale:

Both the risk of infection and the cost of care change with time since transplant, so cases and controls are compared at the same point in their post-transplant course.
Choosing controls among everyone ever transplanted without cryptococcosis would compare cases with people whose follow-up was selected using the future. Risk-set matching uses only what was known at the case’s time zero.

Under the plan, a person who is diagnosed later can serve as a control before their own diagnosis.
Specified in: §5.4 Control eligibility, §6 Matching.
Current code: only people who are never diagnosed are used as controls (#7).

Decision pending: whether one person may serve as a control in more than one risk set, as in standard incidence density sampling, or at most once (D4).



What cases and controls are matched on
Under the plan, whichever matching method is chosen:

cases and controls have the same current graft status (functioning, or failed and on dialysis);
each case has up to 2 controls;
cases are matched in a random order fixed by a recorded seed, and ties between controls are broken at random;
cost in the 3 months before time zero is not used for matching. It is kept to check whether cases and controls had similar costs before diagnosis.

The plan sets out two matching methods, one of each kind described under Ways of matching, and has not chosen between them:

Option A, direct covariate matching: exact matching on diabetes, cirrhosis and HIV, limits on the difference in age and in calendar date, and preference for the control closest in earlier cost (months −12 to −4). Covariates not matched on are checked for balance and, if imbalanced, adjusted for in the outcome model.
Option B, time-varying propensity score matching: a model estimates each person’s probability of being diagnosed in each month from all the covariates in the plan, and each case is matched to the controls with the closest score at the same time since transplant, within 0.2 standard deviations of the logit of the score.

The covariates cover demographics, transplant history, graft function, immunosuppression intensity, comorbidity, other infections, earlier use of care, earlier cost, dual Medicaid eligibility and region, all measured before time zero.
Specified in: §6.1 Common elements, §6.2 Covariates, §6.3 Option A, §6.4 Option B.
Current code: the code implements a form of Option A. Controls are matched exactly on cirrhosis, HIV and diabetes, within 10 years of age and with time zero within 3 years of the case’s, and a control with the same number of transplants is preferred. Each control is used once. It differs from the plan in these ways:

cases are matched in order of how few potential controls they have, not in random order;
among eligible controls, the first in row order is chosen, so the recorded seed has no effect (#3);
graft status and earlier cost are not matched on (#8);
the count of potential controls used to order cases checks Medicare coverage on a different date from the matching itself (#6);
cases for whom no control is found remain in the matched data (#12).


Decision pending: the lookback window for rejection treatment and the comorbidity index (D5); the matching method (D10); and, under Option B, whether to keep the limits on age and calendar date as well (D6).



Checking the match
A flow diagram follows the cohort from the source population through eligibility, case identification and matching, and baseline characteristics are reported by group before and after matching. Balance between cases and controls is judged with standardized mean differences at time zero, for every covariate in the plan and for cost in each of months −3, −2 and −1. An absolute standardized mean difference below 0.1 is taken as adequate. The number of cases with 2, 1 and 0 controls is reported, and unmatched cases are compared with matched ones.
Specified in: §6.5 Matching outcomes reported, §8.1 Descriptive analysis, §8.2 Balance.
