title: Post-match processing
section: Obtain raw costs from raw claims data
text:
Obtain raw costs from raw claims data
We use the usRds functions get_IN_REV_costs(), get_IN_CLM_costs() and get_PS_REV_costs() to extract Medicare claims with payment amounts for 2006 to 2021, for patients in the matched cohort.
The USRDS claims files hold payments at more than one level1:

Institutional claims (inpatient, outpatient, skilled nursing, home health and hospice) come as a claim file, with one row per claim and the Medicare payment for the whole claim (CLM_AMT), and a revenue-center detail file, with one row per revenue center on the claim. get_IN_CLM_costs() reads the claim files and get_IN_REV_costs() the detail files.
Revenue-center lines carry charges (REV_CH) and, for outpatient, home health and hospice claims, a payment (REVPMT). Inpatient and skilled nursing lines have no payment field (Appendix B), so inpatient payments come from the claim file only.
Claim payments and revenue-center payments describe the same services, so adding them would count those services twice. For outpatient claims, summed REVPMT is about 3% higher than CLM_AMT overall1.
Physician/supplier claims are read at the line level: get_PS_REV_costs() returns each line’s payment (PMTAMT), with its submitted and allowed charges. Despite the function’s name, these are line files, not revenue-center files. In the files available to this project, physician/supplier claims before 2013 come as combined files rather than separate claim and line files, as listed in usRds.

The cost outcome uses payment fields (CLM_AMT, REVPMT, PMTAMT), never charges.


Click to show/hide R Code
#Gather raw costs for each patient
costs_raw<-list()
costs_raw[["IN_REV"]]<-get_IN_REV_costs(years = 2006:2021, usrds_ids = post_match_results$USRDS_ID)
costs_raw[["IN_CLM"]]<-get_IN_CLM_costs(years = 2006:2021, usrds_ids = post_match_results$USRDS_ID)
costs_raw[["PS_REV"]]<-get_PS_REV_costs(years = 2006:2021, usrds_ids = post_match_results$USRDS_ID)

title: Post-match processing
text:
Merge cost data to cohort
We take the raw claims data and add it to the previously obtained patient cohort data.
This is done as a nested data frame for convenience in subsequent analysis. A single column is a list, with each element of the list being all cost-related entries for a specific patient. See https://bookdown.org/Maxine/r4ds/nesting.html for more information on nested data in R.
Patients with no observed claims in a given cost category are assigned empty tibbles to ensure consistent downstream processing.
This structure allows costs to be prorated, inflated, and aggregated relative to patient-specific index dates without repeatedly reshaping the data.
While nested data is convenient from many perspectives, it does require the use of the map() family of functions from the purrr package.


Click to show/hide R Code
#Group by ID and nest, so that each patient has a single tibble for each type of cost
#Start with the raw costs
costs_clean <- costs_raw%>% 
  
  #Use the imap function to create nested tibbles so that each USRDS ID is unique
  imap(~.x %>%
         group_by(USRDS_ID) %>%
         nest(!!paste0(.y, "_rows") := -USRDS_ID)
  )%>%
  
  #Join the three tibbles in the resulting list
  reduce(full_join, by = "USRDS_ID")%>%
  
  #Clean up so that patients with empty cost data tibbles do not throw an error later by providing empty columns
  mutate(IN_REV_rows=replace_na(IN_REV_rows, list(tibble(CLM_FROM = as.Date(character()),
                                                         REV_CH = numeric(),
                                                         REVPMT = numeric(),
                                                         HCFASAF = character()))))%>%
  mutate(IN_CLM_rows=replace_na(IN_CLM_rows, list(tibble(CLM_FROM = as.Date(character()),
                                                         CLM_THRU = as.Date(character()),
                                                         CLM_TOT = numeric(),
                                                         CLM_AMT = numeric(),
                                                         HCFASAF = character()))))%>%
  mutate(PS_REV_rows=replace_na(PS_REV_rows, list(tibble(CLM_FROM = as.Date(character()),
                                                         CLM_THRU = as.Date(character()),
                                                         SBMTCH = numeric(),
                                                         ALOWCH = numeric(),
                                                         PMTAMT = numeric(),
                                                         HCFASAF = character()))))



#Add cost tibbles to patients_clean data set
cost_joined<-left_join(post_match_results, 
                       costs_clean, 
                       by = join_by(USRDS_ID))%>%
  mutate(IN_REV_rows=map(IN_REV_rows, ~ if (is.null(.x)) tibble(CLM_FROM = as.Date(character()),
                                                                REV_CH = numeric(),
                                                                REVPMT = numeric(),
                                                                HCFASAF = character()) else .x))%>%
  mutate(IN_CLM_rows=map(IN_CLM_rows, ~ if (is.null(.x)) tibble(CLM_FROM = as.Date(character()),
                                                                CLM_THRU = as.Date(character()),
                                                                CLM_TOT = numeric(),
                                                                CLM_AMT = numeric(),
                                                                HCFASAF = character()) else .x))%>%
  mutate(PS_REV_rows=map(PS_REV_rows, ~ if (is.null(.x)) tibble(CLM_FROM = as.Date(character()),
                                                                CLM_THRU = as.Date(character()),
                                                                SBMTCH = numeric(),
                                                                ALOWCH = numeric(),
                                                                PMTAMT = numeric(),
                                                                HCFASAF = character()) else .x))

title: Post-match processing
section: Costs from start date to end date
text:
Costs from start date to end date
We now write code that totals costs for each patient, accounting for the start and finish dates:

Start: The index date for each patient
Finish: The earliest of

365 days after the index date (maximum_followup)
End of Medicare coverage (minimum 1 day)
Censoring date for end of data (1/1/2022)


Current code: death is not yet an end point of follow-up; it is recorded as the reason follow-up ended only when it falls on one of the dates above (#10). See End of follow-up.
In addition to total costs, we also calculated total costs grouped by type (Inpatient, Outpatient, Home Health, etc.).
Since claims can span many days, we use the prorate_costs_by_day() function from the usRds package to divide the costs evenly among the days spanned by each claim. Proration is applied before date filtering so that only the portion of each claim overlapping the analytic window contributes to total cost.


Click to show/hide R Code
#Now we trial code that accounts for both the start date and the end date
cost_broken_down<-cost_intermediate%>%
  
  #Define end date for purposes of cost using maximum_followup from setup file
  mutate(end_date_analysis=pmin(index_date_match + maximum_followup,
                                censor_date,
                                coverage_end_date,
                                medicare_coverage_end_date,
                                na.rm=TRUE
                                ))%>%
  
  mutate(duration_cost_followup=time_length(interval(index_date_match, end_date_analysis), "days"))%>%
  mutate(follow_up_final_event=case_when(
    end_date_analysis==DIED ~ "Death",
    end_date_analysis==index_date_match + maximum_followup ~ "Maximum follow-up",
    end_date_analysis==censor_date ~ "Censored",
    end_date_analysis==coverage_end_date | end_date_analysis==medicare_coverage_end_date ~ "Loss of coverage"
  ))%>%
  
  #Use pmap_dbl to calculate costs between first_cryptococcus_date and end_date for IN_REV
  mutate(IN_REV_365d_cost_total=pmap_dbl(
    .l=list(IN_REV_rows, index_date_match, end_date_analysis),
    .f=function(claims_df, s_date,e_date) {
      claims_df%>%
        filter(CLM_FROM >= s_date, CLM_FROM<=e_date)%>%
        summarise(total = sum(REVPMT, na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
        pull(total)}
  )
  )%>%
  
  #Same, except now we group by HCFASAF
  #Use pmap to calculate costs between first_cryptococcus_date and end_date for IN_REV, grouped by HCFASAF
  mutate(IN_REV_365d_cost_grouped=pmap(
    .l=list(IN_REV_rows, index_date_match, end_date_analysis),
    .f=function(claims_df, s_date,e_date) {
      claims_df%>%
        filter(CLM_FROM >= s_date, CLM_FROM<=e_date)%>%
        mutate(HCFASAF = stringr::str_replace_all(HCFASAF, " ", ""))%>%
        mutate(HCFASAF = ifelse(HCFASAF=="Inpatient(REBUS)", "Inpatient", HCFASAF))%>%
        mutate(HCFASAF = ifelse(HCFASAF=="Non-claim/auxiliary", "Nonclaimauxiliary", HCFASAF))%>%
        group_by(HCFASAF)%>%
        summarise(total = sum(REVPMT, na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
        pivot_wider(
          names_from  = HCFASAF,
          values_from = total,
          names_prefix = "IN_REV_365d_cost_",
          values_fill = 0
        ) 
      }
  )
  )%>%
  
  #Use pmap_dbl to calculate costs between first_cryptococcus_date and end_date for IN_CLM, after prorating costs by day
  mutate(IN_CLM_365d_cost_total=pmap_dbl(
    .l=list(IN_CLM_rows, index_date_match, end_date_analysis),
    .f=function(claims_df, s_date,e_date) {
      claims_df%>%
        usRds::prorate_costs_by_day()%>%
        filter(CLM_FROM >= s_date, CLM_FROM<=e_date)%>%
        summarise(total = sum(CLM_AMT_PRORATED, na.rm = TRUE))%>%
        pull(total)
    }
      )
  )%>%
  
  
  #Same, except now we group by HCFASAF
  #Use pmap to calculate costs between first_cryptococcus_date and end_date for IN_CLM, after prorating costs by day
  mutate(IN_CLM_365d_cost_grouped=pmap(
    .l=list(IN_CLM_rows, index_date_match, end_date_analysis),
    .f=function(claims_df, s_date,e_date) {
      claims_df%>%
        usRds::prorate_costs_by_day()%>%
        filter(CLM_FROM >= s_date, CLM_FROM<=e_date)%>%
        mutate(HCFASAF = stringr::str_replace_all(HCFASAF, " ", ""))%>%
        mutate(HCFASAF = ifelse(HCFASAF=="Inpatient(REBUS)", "Inpatient", HCFASAF))%>%
        mutate(HCFASAF = ifelse(HCFASAF=="Non-claim/auxiliary", "Nonclaimauxiliary", HCFASAF))%>%
        group_by(HCFASAF)%>%
        summarise(total = sum(CLM_AMT_PRORATED, na.rm = TRUE))%>%
        pivot_wider(
          names_from  = HCFASAF,
          values_from = total,
          names_prefix = "IN_CLM_365d_cost_",
          values_fill = 0
        ) 
    }
  )
  )%>%
  
  
  #Use pmap_dbl to calculate costs between first_cryptococcus_date and end_date for PS_REV
  mutate(PS_REV_365d_cost_total=pmap_dbl(
    .l=list(PS_REV_rows, index_date_match, end_date_analysis),
    .f=function(claims_df, s_date,e_date) {
      claims_df%>%
        filter(CLM_FROM >= s_date, CLM_FROM<=e_date)%>%
        summarise(total = sum(PMTAMT, na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
        pull(total)}
  )
  )%>%
  
  unnest_wider(IN_REV_365d_cost_grouped)%>%
  unnest_wider(IN_CLM_365d_cost_grouped)%>%
  mutate(across(matches("_365d_cost_"), ~replace_na(., 0)))

text:
Accounting for inflation
We repeat the analysis above, except that we use the adjust_costs_for_inflation() function from the usRds package to adjust costs for medical inflation, using the month and year listed in the R/setup.R file to establish the time point at which all costs are anchored based on the medical Consumer Price Index.

Decision pending: which price index is used for inflation adjustment (D7). The code currently uses the medical care component of the Consumer Price Index.



Click to show/hide R Code
cost_inflated<-
  cost_broken_down%>%
  
  #Use pmap_dbl to calculate costs between first_cryptococcus_date and end_date for IN_REV
  mutate(IN_REV_365d_cost_adjusted_total=pmap_dbl(
    .l=list(IN_REV_rows, index_date_match, end_date_analysis),
    .f=function(claims_df, s_date,e_date) {
      claims_df%>%
        filter(CLM_FROM >= s_date, CLM_FROM<=e_date)%>%
        adjust_costs_for_inflation(baseline_month = inflation_month, baseline_year = inflation_year)%>%
        summarise(total = sum(REVPMT_ADJUSTED, na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
        pull(total)}
  )
  )%>%
  
  #Use pmap_dbl to calculate costs between first_cryptococcus_date and end_date for IN_CLM, after prorating costs by day and inflating
  mutate(IN_CLM_365d_cost_adjusted_total=pmap_dbl(

    .f=function(claims_df, s_date,e_date) {

        filter(CLM_FROM >= s_date, CLM_FROM<=e_date)%>%
        summarise(total = sum(CLM_AMT_PRORATED_ADJUSTED, na.rm = TRUE))%>%
        pull(total)
    }
  )
  )%>%
  
  #Use pmap_dbl to calculate costs between first_cryptococcus_date and end_date for PS_REV
  mutate(PS_REV_365d_cost_adjusted_total=pmap_dbl(
    .l=list(PS_REV_rows, index_date_match, end_date_analysis),
    .f=function(claims_df, s_date,e_date) {
      claims_df%>%
        filter(CLM_FROM >= s_date, CLM_FROM<=e_date)%>%
        adjust_costs_for_inflation(baseline_month = inflation_month, baseline_year = inflation_year)%>%
        summarise(total = sum(PMTAMT_ADJUSTED, na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
        pull(total)}
  )
  )%>%
  
  #Same, except now we group by HCFASAF
  #Use pmap to calculate costs between first_cryptococcus_date and end_date for IN_CLM, after prorating costs by day
  mutate(IN_CLM_365d_cost_adjusted_grouped=pmap(
    .l=list(IN_CLM_rows, index_date_match, end_date_analysis),
    .f=function(claims_df, s_date,e_date) {
      claims_df%>%
        usRds::prorate_costs_by_day()%>%
        adjust_costs_for_inflation(baseline_month = inflation_month, baseline_year = inflation_year)%>%
        filter(CLM_FROM >= s_date, CLM_FROM<=e_date)%>%
        mutate(HCFASAF = stringr::str_replace_all(HCFASAF, " ", ""))%>%
        mutate(HCFASAF = ifelse(HCFASAF=="Inpatient(REBUS)", "Inpatient", HCFASAF))%>%
        mutate(HCFASAF = ifelse(HCFASAF=="Non-claim/auxiliary", "Nonclaimauxiliary", HCFASAF))%>%
        group_by(HCFASAF)%>%
        summarise(total = sum(CLM_AMT_PRORATED_ADJUSTED, na.rm = TRUE))%>%
        pivot_wider(
          names_from  = HCFASAF,
          values_from = total,
          names_prefix = "IN_CLM_365d_cost_adjusted",
          values_fill = 0
        ) 
    }
  )
  )%>%
  unnest_wider(IN_CLM_365d_cost_adjusted_grouped)%>%
  mutate(across(matches("_365d_cost_"), ~replace_na(., 0)))

title: Post-match processing
text:
Grouping by month
In order to model costs appropriately, we group costs for each patient into 30-day increments, starting from the beginning of the look-back period defined in the R/setup.R file. This will allow us to estimate full-year costs for patients who lose their coverage or are censored before the end of a full-year but do not experience death.


Click to show/hide R Code
  #Longitudinal data set for modeling
cost_longitudinal<-
  cost_inflated%>%

  #Use pmap to calculate costs between first_cryptococcus_date and end_date for IN_CLM, after prorating costs by day and inflating
  mutate(IN_CLM_365d_cost_adjusted_total_longitudinal=pmap(
    .l=list(IN_CLM_rows, index_date_match, end_date_analysis),
    .f=function(claims_df, s_date,e_date) {
      claims_df%>%
        usRds::prorate_costs_by_day()%>%
        adjust_costs_for_inflation(baseline_month = inflation_month, baseline_year = inflation_year)%>%
        filter(service_date >= s_date-30*baseline_months_cost, service_date<=e_date)%>%
        mutate(month=time_length(interval(s_date, service_date), "days") %/% 30)%>%
        filter(month<12)%>%
        group_by(month)%>%
        summarise(IN_CLM_month_total = sum(CLM_AMT_PRORATED_ADJUSTED, na.rm = TRUE), 
                  .groups = "drop")%>%
        mutate(IN_CLM_month_total=pmax(IN_CLM_month_total,0))%>%
        ungroup()%>%
        tidyr::complete(
          month = full_months
        )
    }
  )
  )%>%

  #Use pmap to calculate costs between first_cryptococcus_date and end_date for PS_REV
  mutate(PS_REV_365d_cost_adjusted_total_longitudinal=pmap(
    .l=list(PS_REV_rows, index_date_match, end_date_analysis),
    .f=function(claims_df, s_date,e_date) {
      claims_df%>%
        filter(CLM_FROM >= s_date-30*baseline_months_cost, CLM_FROM<=e_date)%>%
        adjust_costs_for_inflation(baseline_month = inflation_month, baseline_year = inflation_year)%>%
        mutate(month=time_length(interval(s_date, CLM_FROM), "days") %/% 30)%>%
        filter(month<12)%>%
        group_by(month)%>%
        summarise(PS_REV_month_total = sum(PMTAMT_ADJUSTED, na.rm = TRUE), 
                  .groups = "drop") %>%
        mutate(PS_REV_month_total=pmax(PS_REV_month_total,0))%>%
        ungroup()
    }
        
        
  )
  )%>%

  #IN_CLM, except now we group by HCFASAF
  #Use pmap to calculate costs IN_CLM, after prorating costs by day
  mutate(IN_CLM_365d_cost_adjusted_grouped_longitudinal=pmap(
    .l=list(IN_CLM_rows, index_date_match, end_date_analysis),
    .f=function(claims_df, s_date,e_date) {
      claims_df%>%
        usRds::prorate_costs_by_day()%>%
        adjust_costs_for_inflation(baseline_month = inflation_month, baseline_year = inflation_year)%>%
        filter(service_date >= s_date-30*baseline_months_cost, service_date<=e_date)%>%
        mutate(month=time_length(interval(s_date, service_date), "days") %/% 30)%>%
        filter(month<12)%>%
        mutate(HCFASAF = stringr::str_replace_all(HCFASAF, " ", ""))%>%
        mutate(HCFASAF = ifelse(HCFASAF=="Inpatient(REBUS)", "Inpatient", HCFASAF))%>%
        mutate(HCFASAF = ifelse(HCFASAF=="Non-claim/auxiliary", "Nonclaimauxiliary", HCFASAF))%>%
        group_by(month, HCFASAF)%>%
        summarise(total = sum(CLM_AMT_PRORATED_ADJUSTED, na.rm = TRUE), 
                  .groups = "drop")%>%
        mutate(total=pmax(total,0))%>%
        pivot_wider(
          names_from  = HCFASAF,
          values_from = total,
          names_prefix = "IN_CLM_month_grouped",
          values_fill = 0
        ) 
    }
  )
  )%>%
  mutate(
    cost_column_longitudinal = pmap(
      list(
        IN_CLM_365d_cost_adjusted_total_longitudinal,
        PS_REV_365d_cost_adjusted_total_longitudinal,
        IN_CLM_365d_cost_adjusted_grouped_longitudinal,
        index_date_match, 
        end_date_analysis
      ),
      ~ left_join(..1, ..2, by = "month") %>%
        left_join(..3, by = "month")%>%
        mutate(month_offset=pmin(30, time_length(interval(..4, ..5), "days")-30*month + 1 ))%>%
        mutate(month_offset=pmax(month_offset,0))

    ))%>%
  select(-IN_CLM_365d_cost_adjusted_total_longitudinal,
         -PS_REV_365d_cost_adjusted_total_longitudinal,
         -IN_CLM_365d_cost_adjusted_grouped_longitudinal)%>%
  unnest(cost_column_longitudinal)%>%
  mutate(
    patient_type = factor(patient_type),
    patient_type = relevel(patient_type, ref = "Control")
  )%>%
  
  mutate(across(
    c(
      IN_CLM_month_total,
      PS_REV_month_total,
      starts_with("IN_CLM_month_grouped")
    ),
    ~replace_na(., 0)))%>%
  mutate(grand_total_cost_month=IN_CLM_month_total+PS_REV_month_total)

title: Costs and follow-up
text:
Turning claims into costs

Payments, not charges
Cost is measured as the amount Medicare paid; charges are not used (Payments, not charges). Payments made by patients, other insurers and Medicare Part D are not included.
Two payment fields are used: the Medicare payment on each institutional claim, and the Medicare payment on each physician/supplier line. Outpatient, home health and hospice claims also list payments for each revenue center (each department or type of service on the bill). These describe the same services as the claim’s payment, so the two are never added together.
Specified in: §7.1 Cost measure; exclusions in §11 Limitations. The payment fields and the rule against adding revenue-center payments to claim payments come from the repository’s AGENTS.md.
Current code: a separate 365-day summary also totals revenue-center payments, but separately from the claim totals, not added to them. The monthly costs used in the models come from institutional claim payments and physician/supplier line payments only.


Spreading a stay across days
An institutional claim that covers several days is spread evenly across them (Spreading a stay across days has a worked example).
Specified in: §7.1 Cost measure.
Current code: institutional claims are spread across days in the monthly costs. Physician/supplier lines are assigned to their first day of service. In the separate 365-day summary, institutional costs are spread across days but then selected by the claim’s first day (#11).


Adjusting for inflation
All costs are expressed in January 2021 US dollars.
Specified in: §7.2 Inflation adjustment.
Current code: costs are adjusted with the medical care component of the Consumer Price Index, according to the month in which each claim began.

Decision pending: the price index (D7).



Months, partial months, and missing versus zero
Each person’s follow-up is divided into 30-day months counted from time zero: month 0 is days 0 to 29, month −3 is days −90 to −61, and month 11, the last, is days 330 to 359. A person-month’s cost is the sum of the spread, inflation-adjusted payments for that month. Covered months with no claims count as zero, uncovered months are left out, and partly observed months are kept with their days observed (Missing versus zero cost).
Specified in: §7.3 Person-month structure.
Current code: a monthly total below zero, which can arise from claim adjustments, is set to zero. The plan does not yet describe this step. The separate 365-day summary covers days 0 to 365 (366 days), while the monthly costs cover days 0 to 359 (#13).


End of follow-up
Follow-up ends at the earliest of:

day 365 after time zero;
death;
loss of fee-for-service Medicare as primary payer;
1 January 2022.

Graft failure after time zero does not end follow-up. It is one of the ways cryptococcosis may lead to higher cost.
How death is handled defines what is being estimated (Death and what is estimated). If death ends follow-up, the estimate describes the excess cost of care while people are alive. If the months after death count as zero cost, the estimate also reflects the cost consequences of mortality. Whichever is chosen as primary, the other is a sensitivity analysis.
Specified in: §7.4 End of follow-up.
Current code: follow-up ends at day 365, at 1 January 2022, or at the end of the period of Medicare coverage containing time zero. Death is not yet an end point (#10).

Decision pending: the treatment of death (D8).

title: Execute matching
text:
Overview
The code in this script uses the cohort of kidney transplant patients with and without cryptococcosis developed in the R/create_cohort.R and executes 1:n matching based on a custom-written greedy algorithm
Characteristics of the matching algorithm:

Matching without replacement: each patient without cryptococcosis serves as a control to at most one case, which keeps the later analysis simpler1.
Risk-set sampling (incidence density sampling): if a case develops cryptococcosis 243 days after their most recent kidney transplant, potential controls are chosen on their covariate values at exactly 243 days after their own most recent transplant2.
Greedy matching: each case’s controls are chosen in turn, and earlier choices are not revisited3. Cases are taken in order of how few potential controls they have, a choice made in this code; the order of greedy matching has at most a modest effect on estimates3.
Mix of exact matching and caliper matching

Exact matching on the following:

Cirrhosis
HIV
Diabetes

Caliper matching on the following:

Age (within 10 years on the index date, calculated exactly)
Index date of case and controls (within 3 years of each other)

Preferential matching on the following:

Number of transplants prior to index date




Decision pending: whether a person may serve as a control in more than one risk set (D4).

Current code: potential controls are limited to patients never diagnosed with cryptococcosis, so people diagnosed later cannot serve as controls before their diagnosis (#7). Other differences from the plan, including the order in which cases are matched, are listed under Cases and controls.

title: Execute matching
text:
Create a matched data set
The following code executes the match, creating a matched dataframe suitable for use in subsequent analysis.


Click to show/hide R Code
#Time to set up the matching loop

#Initial the loop control
continue<-TRUE
i<-0
set.seed(12345)

#Initialize the object where the matched cases and controls will be stored
matched_patients<-list()
matched_patients[["Case"]]<-unmatched_patients[["Case"]][0, ]%>%
  mutate(matched_control_indices = list())
matched_patients[["Control"]] <- unmatched_patients[["Control"]][0, ] %>%
  mutate(index_date_match = as.Date(character()))


#Perform the match
while (continue==TRUE)
{
  i<-i+1
  print(i)

  #Select matches from controls
  eligible_controls <-unmatched_patients[["Control"]]%>%
    
    filter(cirrhosis==unmatched_patients$Case$cirrhosis[[1]])%>%
    #filter(CMV==unmatched_patients$Case$CMV[[1]])%>%
    filter(HIV==unmatched_patients$Case$HIV[[1]])%>%
    filter(diabetes==unmatched_patients$Case$diabetes[[1]])%>%
    
    #Risk set matching
    filter(tstart<=unmatched_patients$Case$tstart[[1]])%>%
    filter(tstop>unmatched_patients$Case$tstart[[1]])%>%
    
    #Calculate date for age calculations/etc.
    mutate(.baseline_control_date=unmatched_patients$Case$tstart[[1]] + most_recent_transplant_date)%>%
    
    #Make sure case and control are sampled within 3 years of each other
    filter(abs(time_length(interval(.baseline_control_date, unmatched_patients$Case$cryptococcus_dx_date[[1]]), "years")) <=3)%>%
    
    #filter(cohort_start_date<=unmatched_patients$Case$cryptococcus_dx_date[[1]])%>%
    #filter(cohort_stop_date>unmatched_patients$Case$cryptococcus_dx_date[[1]])%>%
    
    #Age>=18 on index date
    filter(time_length(interval(BORN, .baseline_control_date), "years") >= 18)%>%
    
    #Age difference under 10 years, calculated at sampling date
    filter(abs(time_length(interval(BORN,.baseline_control_date), "years")-
                 time_length(interval(unmatched_patients$Case$BORN[[1]],
                                      unmatched_patients$Case$cryptococcus_dx_date[[1]]), "years")) <=10)%>%
  
    verify_medicare_primary(index_date = ".baseline_control_date", 
                            medicare_coverage_df = medicare_history, 
                            coverage_start_variable = "medicare_coverage_start_date",
                            coverage_end_variable = "medicare_coverage_end_date",
                            cache=TRUE)%>%
    filter(medicare_primary_TF==TRUE)%>%
    
    #Move matches for cumulative number of transplants to the top
    #Note: this step could be used for propensity score matching on various variables
    #Consider minimizing date difference and age difference as well
    arrange(desc(cumulative_transplant_total==unmatched_patients$Case$cumulative_transplant_total[[1]]))
  
  
  #Number of controls is minimum of global constant number_controls_per_case and number of distinct USRDS_IDs
  k <- min(number_controls_per_case, nrow(distinct(eligible_controls, USRDS_ID)))
  
  #Initialize sampled_controls df
  sampled_controls<-eligible_controls[0, ]
    
  #Loop to select controls one at a time to ensure same patient is not sampled multiple times 
  while (k>0)
  {
  
  sampled_controls <- bind_rows(
    sampled_controls,
    eligible_controls %>%slice_head(n = 1))
    
    eligible_controls<-eligible_controls%>%
      filter(!(USRDS_ID %in% sampled_controls$USRDS_ID ))

    k<-min(k-1, nrow(distinct(eligible_controls, USRDS_ID)))   
  }
    
    sampled_controls<-sampled_controls%>%
    mutate(index_date_match = .baseline_control_date)%>%
    select(-.baseline_control_date)
  
  #Add case to matched DF
  matched_patients[["Case"]]<-unmatched_patients$Case[1,]%>%
    mutate(matched_control_indices=list(sampled_controls$USRDS_ID))%>%
    bind_rows(matched_patients[["Case"]])
  
  #Add controls to control DF
  matched_patients[["Control"]]<-matched_patients[["Control"]]%>%
    bind_rows(sampled_controls)
  
  #Remove controls
  unmatched_patients[["Control"]]<-unmatched_patients[["Control"]]%>%
    filter(!(USRDS_ID %in% sampled_controls$USRDS_ID ))
  
  #Remove cases
  unmatched_patients[["Case"]]<-unmatched_patients[["Case"]]%>%
    slice(-1)
  
 if (nrow(unmatched_patients[["Case"]])==0){
   continue<-FALSE
 } 
  
  if (i==10000){
    continue<-FALSE
  }
  
}


post_match_results<-matched_patients%>%
  bind_rows(.id = "patient_type")

title: Execute matching
text:
References


1. Stuart EA. Matching methods for causal inference: A review and a look forward. Stat Sci. 2010;25(1):1-21. doi:10.1214/09-STS313


2. Richardson DB. An incidence density sampling program for nested case-control analyses. Occup Environ Med. 2004;61(12):e59. doi:10.1136/oem.2004.014472


3. Austin PC. A comparison of 12 algorithms for matching on the propensity score. Stat Med. 2014;33(6):1057-1069. doi:10.1002/sim.6004

Project documentsAnalysis plan Code
To comment on any part of this page, highlight the text and use the 💬 Comment button.

1. Objective
To estimate the excess Medicare payments attributable to cryptococcosis in the 12 months after diagnosis among adult kidney transplant recipients, compared with similar recipients at the same time since transplant who have not been diagnosed.
Secondary objectives

Describe the month-by-month profile of excess cost from 3 months before to 12 months after diagnosis.
Partition excess cost by care setting (inpatient, outpatient, skilled nursing, home health, hospice, dialysis, physician/supplier).

2. Design
Retrospective cohort study in linked registry and claims data, using risk-set (incidence density) matching. Each case is matched, at the time since transplant when they are diagnosed, to controls who are still at risk and undiagnosed at that same time.
Decision D10: the matching method — direct covariate matching, or matching on a time-varying propensity score (Section 6).
A sequential target-trial emulation with propensity-score weighting is the planned main sensitivity analysis (Section 9; protocol in Appendix A). It requires a propensity score model whichever matching method is chosen.

3. Data source

United States Renal Data System (USRDS) standard analysis files5, accessed under a data use agreement through the usRds R package.

Core files: patients, transplant (TX), payer history (PAYHIST), treatment history (RXHIST), death.
Transplant files linked from OPTN/UNOS transplant recipient registration (TRR) records for kidney and kidney–pancreas recipients.
Medicare Parts A and B claims: institutional claims and revenue-center lines, and physician/supplier claims. Part D prescription events where a covariate requires them.

Linkage: USRDS links CMS and OPTN records to a single USRDS patient identifier. The study uses this linkage as supplied; no further linkage is performed.
Period: claims 2006–2021; incident cryptococcosis 2007–2020; administrative end of follow-up 2022-01-01.
Geography: United States.

4. Study population

4.1 Source population
Kidney transplant recipients in USRDS with a transplant before 2021.


4.2 Eligibility at time zero (cases and controls alike)
At the risk-set time (Section 5.3), a person is eligible if they:

Have had at least one kidney transplant before that date.
Are aged 18 or older.
Have no prior cryptococcosis diagnosis.
Have Medicare fee-for-service as primary payer for both Part A and Part B for the 365 days before time zero, without gaps, so that baseline covariates and baseline cost are fully observed. Decision D1: whether Medicare as secondary payer or other payer categories are ever eligible.
Are alive and under observation on that date.



4.3 Index transplant
The time scale is time since the most recent kidney transplant before time zero. Retransplant recipients are eligible; prior transplants enter as covariates. Decision D2: inclusion of kidney–pancreas and other multi-organ recipients (exclude, or include with an indicator).

5. Exposure and time zero

5.1 Exposure definition
Incident cryptococcosis, identified from ICD-9-CM and ICD-10-CM diagnosis codes on Medicare institutional or physician/supplier claims. The full code list is published as a supplementary table.
Decision D3: the claim algorithm, meaning the claim types and diagnosis positions accepted and the number of claims required (for example, one inpatient claim, or two outpatient claims within a set window). The choice will cite any available validation literature for fungal infection codes in claims.


5.2 Diagnosis date
The service date of the first qualifying claim.


5.3 Time zero

Cases: the diagnosis date.
Controls: the date on which the control reaches the same number of days since their most recent transplant as the case had at diagnosis.

Eligibility, covariates and baseline cost are measured as of time zero, using only information available before it.


5.4 Control eligibility
Any person meeting Section 4.2 at the case’s risk-set time is eligible, including people who are diagnosed with cryptococcosis later. Their time before diagnosis is unexposed time. Excluding them would condition on the future.
Decision D4: whether a person may serve as a control in more than one risk set (sampling with replacement across risk sets, as in standard incidence density sampling) or at most once.

6. Matching

6.1 Common elements
Whichever method is chosen under D10:

Exact matching on current graft status (functioning, or failed and on dialysis).
Ratio: up to 2 controls per case.
Order: cases are matched in a random order fixed by a recorded seed. Ties among controls are broken at random using the same seed.
Pre-period cost: months −3 to −1 are not used for matching. They are kept to check balance on pre-diagnosis cost6,7.



6.2 Covariates
These are the confounders the design must address. Under Option A (Section 6.3), a subset is matched on directly and the rest are checked for balance. Under Option B (Section 6.4), all enter the score. All are measured before time zero.







Domain
Covariates




Demographics
Age, sex, race and ethnicity, calendar year


Transplant
Time since transplant (the time scale), donor type (living or deceased), retransplant and number of prior transplants, cause of kidney failure, time on dialysis before transplant, induction regimen


Graft function
Current graft status (functioning, or failed and on dialysis)


Immunosuppression intensity
Rejection treatment in the prior 3–6 months; maintenance regimen where observable


Comorbidity
Diabetes, cirrhosis, HIV, other solid organ transplant, a claims-based comorbidity index


Other infections
CMV, BK virus, Pneumocystis pneumonia, other invasive fungal infection, sepsis


Prior use of care
Hospital admissions, emergency visits, skilled nursing days in the prior year


Prior cost
Medicare payments in months −12 to −4, as a smoothed measure (mean or log of monthly cost)


Payer and place
Medicaid dual eligibility, region



Each covariate’s code list or registry field will be specified and published before analysis. Decision D5: the lookback window for rejection treatment, and the comorbidity index (Charlson or Elixhauser).


6.3 Option A: direct covariate matching

Exact matching on diabetes, cirrhosis and HIV status, in addition to graft status.
Calipers on age (±10 years) and calendar time (±3 years), widths chosen for this study.
Among eligible controls, the closest on smoothed prior cost (months −12 to −4) is chosen first.
The remaining covariates in Section 6.2 are checked for balance and, if imbalanced, adjusted for in the outcome model.

Strength: simple to explain and to reproduce. Weakness: exact matching becomes sparse as matching factors are added, so few of the covariates in Section 6.2 can be matched on directly.


6.4 Option B: time-varying propensity score matching

A time-varying propensity score for cryptococcosis diagnosis is estimated on the person-time of the eligible cohort, with a discrete-time logistic model on person-months, which approximates a Cox model with time-varying covariates when the monthly risk is low. Each person-interval’s linear predictor is its score at that time; matching within risk sets on such a score follows Lu, who used a Cox model8.
All covariates in Section 6.2 enter the score.
Controls are chosen by nearest neighbour on the logit of the score, within a caliper of 0.2 standard deviations of the logit, the width Austin recommended for a score estimated at baseline9.
Decision D6: whether to keep the hard calipers on age and calendar time from Option A on top of the score.

Strength: balances many covariates at once, and the same score model serves the target-trial sensitivity analysis. Weakness: depends on a correctly specified score model and is harder to explain.


6.5 Matching outcomes reported

The number of cases with 2, 1 and 0 matched controls.
The characteristics of unmatched cases compared with matched cases.

7. Outcome

7.1 Cost measure
Medicare paid amounts (not charges) from institutional claims and physician/supplier claims. Institutional claims spanning several days are prorated evenly across days of service.


7.2 Inflation adjustment
All costs are expressed in January 2021 US dollars. Decision D7: the price index (for example, the medical care component of the CPI-U, or the PCE health price index).


7.3 Person-month structure

Each person’s follow-up is divided into 30-day months relative to time zero, from month −3 (days −90 to −61) through month 11 (days 330 to 359).
Each person-month’s cost is the sum of prorated, inflation-adjusted payments for services in that month.
Partial months are kept, with the number of observed days recorded as exposure.
A month with Medicare coverage and no claims has a cost of zero. A month without qualifying coverage is not observed; it is never recorded as zero cost.



7.4 End of follow-up
Follow-up ends at the earliest of:

day 365 after time zero;
death;
loss of Medicare fee-for-service primary coverage for Parts A and B;
the administrative end date, 2022-01-01.

Graft failure after time zero does not end follow-up; it is an outcome pathway, not a censoring event.
Decision D8: the treatment of death, which defines the estimand. In option (a), cost accrues only while alive, and death ends follow-up. In option (b), months after death count as zero cost, so the estimand includes the cost consequences of mortality. Whichever is primary, the other is a sensitivity analysis.

8. Statistical analysis

8.1 Descriptive analysis

A cohort flow diagram from the source population through eligibility, case identification, and matching.
Baseline characteristics at time zero, by group, before and after matching.



8.2 Balance

Standardized mean differences at time zero for every covariate in Section 6.2, and for cost in months −3, −2 and −1.
An absolute standardized mean difference below 0.1 is considered adequate balance.
Balance on months −3 to −1, which were not matched on, is reported as a check on residual confounding.



8.3 Estimand
The average treatment effect in the treated (ATT): the mean difference in total Medicare payments over months 0–11 between cases and their matched controls, per case.


8.4 Primary model

Person-month cost is modelled with a generalized linear model with log link and Tweedie variance, including group, month (as a categorical variable), and their interaction, with log observed days as an offset.
Standard errors are estimated with generalized estimating equations clustered on matched set; robust standard errors also cluster on patient if D4 allows a person in more than one set.
Retransformation to dollars: predicted monthly cost for each group is computed at a full 30-day month by recycled predictions. The ATT is the sum of case-minus-control differences over months 0–11.
Confidence intervals come from a cluster bootstrap that resamples matched sets (1,000 replicates, or more if needed for stability).
Decision D9: whether the primary estimate subtracts the pre-period difference (months −3 to −1), giving a difference-in-differences, or relies on matching alone with the pre-period reported as a balance check.



8.5 Secondary analyses

The month-by-month excess cost profile for months −3 to 11, from the primary model.
Excess cost by care setting, using the same model on each setting’s cost.



8.6 Missing data

Cost outcomes are observed only during covered months, by design (Section 7.3).
For covariates with missing registry values, missingness is described. If it exceeds 5% for any covariate in the score (a threshold chosen for this study), multiple imputation by chained equations10 is used, with the score estimated within each imputation.



8.7 Software
Analyses are run in R. Code is public at https://github.com/VagishHemmige/Cryptococcus-cost-analysis, and a website at https://vagishhemmige.github.io/Cryptococcus-cost-analysis documents each step. Data are not shared, as the data use agreement requires.

9. Sensitivity analyses

Sequential target-trial emulation (Appendix A). Monthly trials of everyone eligible, with the newly diagnosed as the exposed group. The comparison group is weighted by propensity odds (ATT weights), trials are pooled, and robust standard errors are clustered on patient. Weights are truncated at the 1st and 99th percentiles, with untruncated results also reported.
Alternative death handling: the option in D8 not chosen as primary.
Alternative outcome models: Gaussian identity-link and log-cost models, to show sensitivity to distributional assumptions.
Alternative exposure algorithm: a stricter claims definition than D3 (for example, requiring an inpatient claim), to address misclassification.
Matching variations: a 1:1 ratio; exact matching on CMV status; under Option B, a caliper of 0.1 standard deviations. The matching method not chosen under D10 may also be run as a sensitivity analysis.
Restriction to first transplant recipients.
Pre-2015 and 2015-or-later diagnoses, to check stability across the ICD-9-CM to ICD-10-CM transition (October 2015).

10. Disclosure control

No cell with a count under 11 is reported in any table, figure, or text, including flow diagrams and website pages. Complementary cells are suppressed where they would allow a small count to be derived.
Figures that show individual-level data (for example, beeswarm or scatter plots) are not published.
All outputs are reviewed against the USRDS data use agreement before release.

11. Limitations to address in reporting

Claims-based diagnoses carry misclassification of both exposure and covariates.
Costs are Medicare payments only; patient cost-sharing, other payers, and Part D are excluded unless Part D is added.
Restricting to Medicare fee-for-service primary coverage limits generalizability to recipients with other primary payers or Medicare Advantage.
Confounding by unmeasured immunosuppression intensity may remain despite the covariates in Section 6.2.
Coverage requirements depend on eligibility rules that change over time, such as the end of Medicare entitlement 36 months after a successful transplant for patients without another qualifying reason.

title: Methodological background
text: This page explains, in general terms and without code, the data and methods a study like this one rests on: what the United States Renal Data System and Medicare claims are, how claims become costs, how comparison patients are chosen, and why cost data need particular models. What this study chose, and how its code stands against its plan, is on Study design and methods.

title: Methodological background
section: The United States Renal Data System

title: Methodological background
text:
Medicare claims
A claim is a bill submitted to Medicare for a service. There are two kinds1:

Institutional claims are bills from facilities: hospital inpatient stays, hospital outpatient care, skilled nursing facilities, home health agencies, hospices and dialysis facilities. Each claim covers one stay or episode, with dates from its first to its last day of service.
Physician/supplier claims are bills from clinicians, laboratories and suppliers. Each line of a claim is one service.

title: Methodological background
text:
Medicare as primary payer
Medicare claims give a complete picture of a person’s care only when traditional (fee-for-service) Medicare pays first. When a Medicare Advantage plan or an employer’s insurance pays first, many services never appear in the Medicare claims, so the USRDS recommends building claims-based cohorts from periods when Medicare is the primary payer1.
For a month outside a period of fee-for-service primary coverage, the Medicare claims are incomplete: care may have been billed to someone else. Such a month cannot be treated as a month with no cost.
Many kidney transplant recipients lose Medicare coverage over time: Medicare entitlement based only on kidney failure ends with the 36th month after the month of transplant2, unless the person qualifies another way (for example by age or disability).

title: Methodological background
text:
Finding a diagnosis in claims
A claim shows that a clinician recorded a diagnosis for billing. It does not show that the diagnosis was confirmed, and codes are sometimes recorded while a diagnosis is being ruled out. Diagnoses identified from claims are therefore sometimes wrong3. For invasive aspergillosis in stem cell and solid organ transplant recipients, for example, the positive predictive value of single ICD-9 codes against medical-record review was 15% for one code and 71% for another4. We found no comparable validation study of cryptococcosis codes.

title: Methodological background
text:
Risk-set matching
In risk-set matching (also called incidence density sampling), each case is compared with people drawn from its risk set5: everyone who, at the point the case is diagnosed on the study’s time scale (for example, time since transplant), is still eligible and has not been diagnosed. That point is the case’s time zero, the date from which outcomes are counted, and controls are given the same time zero.
Because controls are chosen using only what was known at time zero, a person who is diagnosed later can serve as a control before their own diagnosis. Their time before diagnosis is unexposed time, and excluding them would condition on the future and bias the comparison6.

title: Methodological background
text:
Ways of matching
Two common ways to choose controls within a risk set are:

Direct covariate matching: matching on the characteristics themselves, for example exactly on some and within set limits on others.
Propensity score matching: a model estimates each person’s probability of being diagnosed from their characteristics, and each case is matched to controls with a similar score7. When the probability is estimated over time, the score is time-varying8.

A common check of whether cases and controls are similar after matching is the standardized mean difference of each characteristic9.

title: Methodological background
text:
Payments, not charges
Charges, which are the prices providers list on their bills, are much higher than what is paid, and they are a poor measure of cost10.
Outpatient, home health and hospice claims also list payments for each revenue center (each department or type of service on the bill). These describe the same services as the claim’s payment, so the two should not be added together1.

title: Methodological background
text:
Spreading a stay across days
An institutional claim that covers several days can be spread evenly across them; this study does so. For example, a 10-day hospital stay with a Medicare payment of $20,000 counts as $2,000 per day. If the stay runs from 2 days before time zero to 7 days after it, $4,000 falls before time zero and $16,000 after it.

title: Methodological background
text:
Missing versus zero cost

A month in which the person is covered but has no claims has a cost of zero: had they needed care, Medicare would have paid for it.
A month in which the person is not covered is not observed, and is left out rather than recorded as zero, because its claims are incomplete1.
A month that is only partly observed, because follow-up ended partway through, is kept. The number of days observed is recorded, so the analysis can account for it.

title: Methodological background
text:
Death and what is estimated
How death is handled defines what is being estimated. If death ends follow-up, the estimate describes the cost of care while people are alive. If the months after death count as zero cost, the estimate also reflects the cost consequences of mortality. How death and incomplete follow-up are handled is a central issue in estimating costs over a period of illness11.
